articles.title: The Best Deals Today: Control Resonant, Apple AirPods Pro 3, 4K Blu-ray Sales, and More
articles.content:
A new weekend has arrived, and today, you can save big on Control Resonant, Saros, the Criterion Collection sale, Gears of War: E-Day, Dragon Ball Super, Apple Watch Ultra 4, Xenoblade Chronicles 2, Persona 3 Reload, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, Star Wars Zero Company, and more. Check out our top picks for Sunday, November 15, below.

AirPods Pro 3 for $179.99

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are on sale today for $179.99, which is a nice $80 off the typical price at Amazon. These earbuds are excellent, with vastly improved ANC technology from previous generations. Plus, there's a built-in heart rate sensor that can track your vitals during workouts.

Control Resonant for $49.99

Control Resonant is one of the most popular games of 2026, and today, you can save $10 off a physical copy. In our 8/10 review, we wrote, "Even when combat's sharp edge eventually dulls, Control Resonant is a great addition to the Remedyverse. While its story follows a more standard framework, its gravitational pull is in the inventive world built around it and the humanization that grounds the paranatural intrigue."

Save $700 Off this Asus TUF A16 Gaming Laptop

It's no secret that building a gaming PC is more expensive than ever. Component prices for parts like RAM are through the roof, which has led many to hold off upgrading their builds. Today, while not a desktop, you can save $700 on this Asus TUF gaming laptop that features a Ryzen 7 8745HX processor, 16GB of RAM, and an RTX 5060. Not bad if you're looking to play some of the latest games on the go.

Saros for $41.99

Saros is on sale for $41.99 today at Amazon, which matches the lowest price we've seen so far. As one of the biggest PS5 exclusives in 2026, now is a great time to check out Housemarque's latest if you haven't. In our review, we wrote, "With Saros, Housemarque once again proved that its bullet-hell sensibilities mesh incredibly well with fluid and super-challenging action. This is primarily a test of skill that's as much a rhythmic dance as it is a fireworks show with a punch-packing sci-fi arsenal."

Sony INZONE H9 Wireless Gaming Headset for $178

Amazon has the Sony Inzone H9 headset on sale for $178 today, which is a huge discount from its standard $329.99 price tag. In our 8/10 review, we wrote, "Sony’s InZone H9 II is a super comfortable and smartly designed headset that shines specifically in competitive gaming, but carries a demanding price tag. It's stiff competition at the high-end, but this headset does some things better than most."

50% Off Criterion Collection Sale

Barnes & Noble is having a Criterion Collection sale right now, so this weekend is one of the best times of the year to pick up some new 4K Blu-rays. Oftentimes, these 4K transfers are overseen by the original Director, and there's always plenty of great extras included.

Frankenstein 4K UHD for $29.98

Frankenstein finally hit 4K Blu-ray as part of The Criterion Collection last month, and today, you can take home a copy for just $29.98. In our 9/10 review, we wrote, "Guillermo del Toro’s Frankenstein is a crowning achievement for the beloved genre director and one of the most effective adaptations of the Mary Shelley story ever put to film."

Gears of War: E-Day for $60.99

Gears of War: E-Day is one of the best games of the year, and today, you can save a few dollars on a physical Xbox copy at Amazon. We gave the game a 9/10 in our review, writing, "Gears of War: E-Day’s stellar story campaign is complemented by an excellent multiplayer suite, particularly its evolved Horde Siege PvE mode."

Save Big on Dragon Ball Super

Amazon has the Dragon Ball Super Complete Series Blu-ray on sale for $116.25 today. This collection includes ten Steelbooks and 20 discs, with a variety of special and bonus features available in addition to the 131 episodes.

Save $100 Off Apple Watch Ultra 4

Amazon has the Apple Watch Ultra 4 smartwatch on sale for $799.99 this weekend. This saves you $100 off MSRP. You'll get the Black Titanium Case and the Black Titanium Milanese Loop with this watch, which can easily complement any outfit. If you've been on the hunt for a new smartwatch, the Ultra 4 is one of the best you can buy.

Dune: Awakening for $39.99

Physical PS5 copies of Dune: Awakening are on sale for $39.99 right now at Amazon. This is the perfect time to jump in, especially with Dune: Part Three just a few months away. In our 8/10 review, we wrote, "Dune: Awakening is an excellent survival MMO that captures Frank Herbet’s sci-fi world incredibly well, mostly to its advantage and occasionally to its detriment. The survival climb from dehydrated peasant to powerful warlord of Arrakis is a joy almost every step of the way, and the story and worldbuilding filled this nerd with absolute joy."

Xenoblade Chronicles 2 + Expansion Pass Bundle for $39.94

Xenoblade Chronicles 2 is one of my favorite games of all time. The expansive world, gripping narrative, incredible cast, and spectacular soundtrack are just a few of the things you can look forward to in this adventure. Walmart has a digital bundle of both the base game and the Expansion Pass (which includes Torna: The Golden Country) on sale for $39.94. If you have a Switch 2, you can then upgrade your copy to the Switch 2 Edition for $10, which adds 4K and 60 FPS support. I cannot recommend this one enough, especially if you're a fan of JRPGs.

The Super Mario Galaxy Movie 4K for $12.99

The Super Mario Galaxy Movie is one of the best performing movies of 2026, and today, you can score the Collector's Edition 4K for only $12.99 at Amazon. This package includes the movie on 4K, Blu-ray, and digital, so you can watch it however you'd like. There's also over an hour of special features to check out, too.

Persona 3 Reload (Switch 2) for $24.99

Persona 3 Reload Switch 2 copies are available at Amazon for $24.99 this weekend. This is a pretty great price for an expansive RPG that you can easily sink 100 hours into. The Switch 2 version had a rocky launch with frame pacing issues, but those have been resolved. Atlus also did add support for 60 FPS in docked mode.

Primetime 4K Up for Pre-Order

Amazon has opened pre-orders for the Primetime 4K Blu-ray, which is due out January 26. In our 9/10 review, we wrote, "A blast from the past with a sickly allure, the Robert Pattinson romp Primetime is as garish as its subject: Chris Hansen’s To Catch a Predator."

Star Wars Zero Company for $47.97

Star Wars Zero Company is one of the biggest sleeper hits of the year, and you can save $12 off a physical copy today at Amazon. In our 9/10 review, we wrote, "Star Wars Zero Company is an excellent tactical game that does a fantastic job of slathering on the same cinematic look and feel we saw in Respawn's Star Wars Jedi games, incorporating strong characters and a storyline that's refreshingly centered on non-Force users and a non-traditional villain."

Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter for $39.99

Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter is the first entry in the beloved Trails series, and last year's remake brought new life to the original game. With 2nd Chapter out now, today is a great time to dive into this wonderful RPG series.

articles.title: 30 must-have PC tool gifts for hobbyists and makers
articles.description: Whether you're a PC builder or a hobbyist with a 3D printer, you'll need tools to build, clean, repair and complete your projects. Here are some of the best ones you can pick up for a techie over this holiday season.
articles.content:
It's fun to build a PC. This is Tom's Hardware, after all. While the AI boom has forced prices to go up and up, there's still a lot of fun to be had putting a build together. Researching your parts, weighing up the pros and cons, then putting it all together. Seeing your brand new PC pass its first boot test, waiting to see if it'll actually load and not just beep and stay blank, is always a thrill.

To get to that point, though, you're going to need some kit. You'll need tools to build, but also to maintain, clean, and repair: your PC is going to need it all at some stage. I've built my own toolkit over the years. My go-to right now is a Hoto screwdriver, but I've got electric dusters, flashlights, screw kits, the lot, all ready for a project or two. My toolkit is versatile enough that it's helped me just as much while I renovate my home as it has in putting together my last build.

● Check out all the PC tool deals on Amazon

My toolkit is pretty expansive these days, but if you or a loved one is just starting out, you'll probably be wondering what to buy. I've put together a mix of the must-buys and nice-to-haves below for any PC builder, maker, and hobbyist's toolkit to help you decide.

If you're not a hobbyist yourself, these tools would make great gifts to share over the holiday season, too!

Screwdrivers and Hand Tools

Everyone needs a decent screwdriver. I've been daily-driving my Hoto electric screwdriver all year, and several of my Tom's Hardware colleagues swear by them. I've got a whole set of manual and precision screwdrivers for general DIY, with my Hoto for keeping my PC in good working order.

Here's some of the kit that we'd recommend you buy to get started.

25-in-1 Mini Electric Screwdriver: was $39.99 now $31.99
A simple, go-to screwdriver set for the office, workshop, and your go-bag. With all the bits you will need to fix a multitude of problems. And now it's on sale for 25% off MSRP. View Deal

Si Pro Electric Screwdriver: was $49.97 now $39.99
With this Fanttik S1 Pro electric screwdriver, you're get 16 S2 steel bits and a driver with three torque settings (from 1.5 to 4.2N.m). You get the screwdriver, storage case, bits, USB-C charging cable, and a manual. View Deal

PixelDrive Electric Screwdriver: was $79.99 now $63.99
The Hoto PixelDrive is a magnetic, precision cordless screwdriver powered by a 2,500 mAh battery and charged via a USB-C cable. An upgrade over the Tom's Hardware favorite, the Nex O1 Pro, this model includes a built-in LCD screen to display torque and battery levels. It weighs 317g, features six different torque settings, and includes 30 different ultra-hard screw bits. View Deal

155 Piece Electronics Toolkit: was $59.99 now $41.99
This 155-pirece kit has everything you need to get started with your first, or next, PC build. You get a precision screwdriver with 140 different bits (slot, Phillips, Pozidrive, Pentalobe, Torx, nut driver, Gamebit (for Nintendo consoles), Torx / Torx security, and many others. You also get spudgers and pry tools, and even a suction cup. View Deal

NEX O1 PRO 3.6V Screwdriver Set: was $49.99 now $29.98
This is my go-to driver and a popular one with Tom's Hardware staffers. The Hoto NEX O1 Pro is a magnetic precision electric screwdriver powered by a 1,500 mAh battery that will drive over 1,000 screws on a single USB-C charge. There are 25 different bits included in the case. This kit comes with a sturdy box and all the bits you will need to keep your PC running. View Deal

164-in-1 Precision Screwdriver Set: was $29.99 now $22.99
This kit has all of the bits that you will ever need to keep your 3D printer, laptop, or PC running smoothly, and you get a great case to keep it all in. View Deal

HOTO SNAPBLOQ S-A01 3.7V Electric Screwdriver: was $99.99 now $79.99
This HOTO SnapBloq 3.7V electric screwdriver includes 56 bits including Slotted, Phillips, Hexagon, Hexagon Security, Torx, Torx Security, Pentalobe, Standoff, Y-Shaped, Tri-Wing, Triangle, Square, U-Shaped, JIS, SIM Card Needle. It also has three torque settings, an integrated light, and charges via USB-C. View Deal

Wera is a quality brand for tools. These long arm, ball-headed hex keys provide all the key metric sizes from 1.5 to 10mm. If you're a DIYer with plenty of furniture to put together, you'll want a set like this at your disposal. View Deal

Manta: $69.95
All the bits that you need to take a PC apart or build IKEA furniture. This iFitit kit comes with a great mix of precision 4mm bits for general electronics and small projects, and 1/4 inch bits for the larger jobs. You get drivers for both sizes and the same magnetic case as the Make, to prevent losing screws as you take things apart. View Deal

Flush Cutters: $7.49
Trim, cut, and rip plastic and soft metal from places where it shouldn’t be. Use these cutters to trim electronic components or for other craft projects. I've used a set like this when I'm 3D printing and need to snip off a few extra parts I don't need on a model, for instance. View Deal

Complete Master Workstation Set: $69.99
This Hoto workstation set is the go-to kit for on-the-go DIYers, PC builders, and hobbyists. It comes in a magnetic case which helps to organize 26 different steel precision kits, six spudgets, five opening picks, two tweezers, a suction cup, and a pry knife.

You're also getting a magnetic pad, anti-static wrist strap, along with demagnetizing and magnetizing zones. It comes with an electric driver with a 350 mAh battery, rechargeable using USB-C, that's ultra-slim and porable. View Deal

4-Piece 12-inch Long Screwdriver Set Slotted and Phillips, Long & Short Magnetic Screwdriver Set: $8.54
Don't underestimate the importance of a long screwdriver. If you're taking something apart, or you're trying to get deep into a PC case, a set like this means you don't have to try and reach in with your hands. It makes the job a whole lot simpler, and it's magnetic, so you shouldn't lose the screws while you're doing it, too. View Deal

Screw Kits

A good driver needs a good set of screws. I can't tell you how many screws I've lost at the worst times when I'm putting a PC together or making a repair. With one of these kits, you won't have to worry. You'll have hundreds of screws, all in different sizes, that you can pull out when you need to.

500-Piece Computer Screw Kit: was $9.99 now $8.99
Another huge kit of PC screws you'll need for every eventuality, although with some thermal paste you can call on for emergencies. View Deal

With ten different types of screws, stand-offs, and gaskets, this kit has everything you need to secure your precious components inside your PC. And now you can get them on sale. View Deal

1595 Pcs Metric Screw Assortment Kit: $18
A huge 1,595 set of screws, nuts and bolts, as well as washers, four hex wrenches, and tweezers. This is a good kit for a DIYer or builder. View Deal

Soldering Irons and Maker Tools

Makers need the right tools to bring together their projects. A good-quality portable soldering iron is essential, especially if you're fixing any electronics. There's also rotary tools and impact power drills for the more intensive jobs in your to-do list.

With 100W of soldering power in such a small package, the HS-02B is a powerful tool for precision soldering and for times when we really need to lay down the heat to melt beefy solder joints. View Deal

This Hoto 16V cordless drill delivers 50 newton-meter torque, with dual high-speed modes providing between 400 and 1,700 RPM for drilling and driving. It's fully rechargeable, with a 1,900 mAh battery. It comes with 10 screwdriver bits, two metal drill bits, three woodworking bits, a multi-purpose ceramic bit, and an extension rod with storage. The rotary tool itself is fitted with a high speed motor, offering five speed modes between 5,000 and 25,000 RPM. You can use this for sanding, polishing, cutting, carving, as well as to finish off a 3D printed model. It's battery operated, using USB-C for charging, and has a full array of attachments for various roles. View Deal

Flashlights

You won't worry about having a flashlight until you need it. Looking deep inside a PC case, trying to repair under a cabinet, lost power during a power cut, or stuck outside in the dark: you'll want a light source you can rely on that isn't going to be a drain on your phone's battery.

This is where one of these portable flashlights come in. They're all rechargable, bright and with long battery lives to get you through a project or a crisis.

IMINI 2 Flashlight: $19.99
This compact and easy to use flashlight provides 50 Lumens of light, without the need to fiddle around for a button. Just unclip, and your flashlight is ready to light your way. View Deal

This Hoto model is rechargeable over USB-C and comes with up to 90 hours of battery life, thanks to its 3,100 mAh battery. Brightness provided is up to 1,000 Lumens. Air Dusters and Cleaning Tools

Cleaning is one of those PC maintenance tasks that we've all probably left until our PC cases are fill with dust and grime, not to mention our keyboards and mice. A good set of cleaning tools, especially an air duster, can make all the difference. Blast it all out, and give it a nice clean brush down, and you'll help to keep your machine running in top working order.

These tools are versatile, so you can use them whenever you need to defeat some dust and grime, whether it's your car dashboard or your project room.

articles.title: GTA 6's Jason and Lucia Will Start as Small-Time Criminals Who Have to Work Up to High-Value Jobs
articles.description: GTA 6 will let Jason and Lucia pull off high-value jobs, but Rockstar Games asks players to work up from being small-time criminals first.
articles.content:
GTA 6 will let Jason and Lucia pull off high-value jobs, but Rockstar Games asks players to work up from being small-time criminals first.

The latest peek at this week's new Grand Theft Auto game arrived courtesy of a preview piece from The Guardian (via @GameRoll_ ). It included interviews with Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson and head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe, who covered the kind of people GTA 6 will cater to and the kind of people it's about.

Jason and Lucia are two names we've heard for years, and they're not about to go away any time soon. After 13 years, faithful GTA fans will soon finally go hands-on with the next mainline game in the groundbreaking open-world sandbox series. They won't be able to immediately pull off front-page heists out of the gate, though.

The Guardian said players won't be allowed to have the duo rob Vice City jewelry stores or drive around Leonida in sports cars in the early moments of GTA 6. Instead, they'll only be able to "hotwire low-end vehicles and pick basic locks" until they work their way up to high-value work later. What the threshold to reach those moments is remains unclear, but considering Rockstar has toiled away on the game for more than a decade, it's probably best that players don't burn their way to the top too quickly.

Nelson described the "younger couple" as a pair with "their backs against the wall" when we first meet them. We've known that GTA 6 takes after Red Dead Redemption 2 in some respects, so Jason and Lucia won't be whipping out RPGs from their back pocket – at least at first. The piece added that robbing everything from gas stations to upscale mall boutiques might be easier or more fruitful if players take the time to complete extra steps. That might mean disabling security cameras or stealing surveillance footage, or it could mean scoping out locations for more discreet entry points.

Skip the prep and a robbery might get chaotic quickly. That's where thinking on your toes will prove beneficial not only for your success but for Jason and Lucia, too. Judging by some of the Wanted System changes Rockstar has detailed in the past, players might want to think twice before making any knee-jerk reactions.

A more detailed and realistic world line with another new element Rockstar accounted for: empathy. As detailed by The Guardian, Nelson and the rest of the team have promised that GTA 6 includes "mechanisms for encouraging" empathy for the first time in series history. What exactly that means remains to be seen, but with many details and different ways to play, we probably won't fully understand the developers' vision until we meet Jason and Lucia ourselves.

GTA 6 launches for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S November 19. For more, you can check out IGN's preview from earlier this year. You can also check out the recent leak that spilled the full track list for the game's official album, and why we're excited to jump into Vice City, even if it's at 30 fps.

articles.title: Nvidia engineer leaves company over lack of transparency around Jensen Huang’s exit, details decision
articles.description: Dai's post shows how much Nvidia employees looked up to the former CEO.
articles.content:
Just days after Jensen Huang suddenly resigned from his position at Nvidia, an Nvidia Robot Research Engineer said that he would leave the company as well. But more than just showing support for the former CEO with a generic “I stand with Jensen” message, Darrel Dai laid out several reasons for the decision on X.

I’ve decided to leave NVIDIA. There are a few things I want to say.As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the company’s CEO.I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious. He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority. Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI.I have seen that same vision in physical AI: investing in robotics, sharing open-source tools and projects, and building computing platforms that bring AI into the physical world. This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in.But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build.Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.That is why this has been so disappointing.I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny.What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me.I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.I understand that some information cannot be shared immediately. But that does not erase the feeling of being left outside a decision that affects the company we help build every day.A company’s greatness comes from its leadership, its governance, and the people who turn its ambitions into reality. Employees’ trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too.Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close.I leave with sadness and gratitude. The colleagues I have worked with, and the work we believed in together, will always matter to me.These are my personal views. November 15, 2026

“What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me,” the engineer posted. “I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.”

It seems that Jensen Huang has gained the respect of the people working under him, with many calling for his reinstatement despite the many controversies he is currently facing. There’s also an online petition demanding that the Nvidia board “Bring Jensen Back,” with over 150,000 signatures at the time of writing.

Nvidia is centered around Jensen Huang, with the former chief executive reportedly having a small army of 60 people directly reporting to him. But despite his busy schedule and legendary persona, Dai said that “Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly,” and that “It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.” Dai also pointed out that “employees’ trust and sense of belonging” are part of what makes a company great. More importantly, Nvidia is known as one of the tech companies with the most generous pay packages. Jensen was even quoted saying, “I pay my employees as much as I can.”

It remains unclear what the former Nvidia CEO will do after all these issues. Elon Musk has already said on X that “it would be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang, especially as he’s embarking on his own ambitious chipmaking journey. As for the employees left behind at Nvidia, some are staying and have shown their full support to interim CEO Colette Kress, while many more want him back. However, there has also been talk that various Silicon Valley tech and semiconductor firms are aggressively attempting to poach Nvidians, although these are just rumors so far.

articles.title: Cockpit-Simulator 737X CDU (v2) Review: An Essential Component for Flight Sim Enthusiasts
articles.description: The CS 737X CDU (v2) by Cockpit-Simulator is a plug-and-play, 1:1 replica of a Boeing 737 Control Display Unit for home cockpit builds.
articles.content:
Thanks to the popularity of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, followed by Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, a growing number of companies have entered the flight simulation peripheral market — offering everything from budget-friendly products to high-end equipment designed for professional and home cockpits.

Cockpit-Master and Cockpit-Simulator were jointly founded in 2018 to develop and manufacture flight simulation equipment. In 2024, the company was split into two divisions, with Cockpit-Simulator focusing on more premium, professional-grade equipment.

Today, we are looking at the CS 737X CDU v2, a 1:1 replica of the Boeing 737 Control Display Unit (CDU). We will examine its build quality, how closely it replicates the real 737 CDU, and how well it integrates with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

The Real Boeing 737 Control Display Unit

Before taking a look at the product itself, let’s first look at the real 737 Control Display Unit (CDU) and explain its functionality.

The CDU is the primary interface pilots use to interact with the aircraft’s Flight Management System (FMS). The FMS can be thought of as the aircraft’s “brain,” handling a wide range of navigation and performance-related tasks. Pilots use the CDU to enter and modify the flight plan, while the FMS calculates the lateral route and vertical profile of the flight. It also manages performance calculations, monitors fuel and flight progress, and provides guidance to the autopilot.

(Image credit: flaps2approach.com) The CDU features a display screen with six line select keys on either side. These keys allow pilots to select and enter information into specific fields on the display, including data entered into the scratchpad. The CDU also includes dedicated function keys for tasks such as accessing performance information and entering instrument departures and approaches. Below the display is an alphanumeric keypad, which pilots use to enter text and other data before transferring it to the selected field using the line select keys.

Build Quality

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Unlike other consumer grade CDUs on the market, the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a full-metal, CNC-machined aluminum shell.

The buttons are made of silicone rubber, which also closely replicates what we felt in our time on a 737 simulator.

The display is where we noticed the biggest departure from the real 737 CDU. The real unit uses a thick, chemically strengthened, anti-glare optical glass cover, whereas the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a standard commercial display. As a result, there is some glare, although the display itself is excellent and offers very wide viewing angles. Despite this difference, the visual presentation is remarkably close to that of the real 737 CDU. The font styling, image sharpness, and color reproduction all closely match what you would see on the real flight deck.

The CS 737X CDU v2 also features a handle, which on the real aircraft is used for the maintenance crew to remove the CDU. This isn’t entirely necessary in a home setup, but it is a nice touch.

The unit can be easily placed on a desk using the included desktop stand, or integrated directly into a larger cockpit setup.

The Feel

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The weight, rigidity, and metallic construction closely replicate the feel of the CDU we experienced in a 737 simulator. The silicone buttons also require a firm, deliberate press to actuate, helping prevent accidental double-inputs during turbulence. This tactile resistance closely matches the experience of using the real unit. Manually entering a long route, rather than importing it from SimBrief, will give your fingers a workout – and will give you a newfound appreciation for the import button.

Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) For our testing inside of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, we used the PMDG 737-800. We flew the following routes:

45 minutes from Las Vegas, Nevada to Ontario, California

2 hours from Phoenix, Arizona to San Francisco, California

5 hours from Oakland, California to Honolulu, Hawaii

This allowed us to examine how the CS 737X CDU v2 handles routes of various duration.

For hardware, the device only requires a USB connection. It also requires the CockpitSimulator Bridge, which needs to be left open throughout the flight. This can be downloaded from the official Cockpit-Simulator site.

Our flow was similar in each case:

Import the flight plan from SimBrief

Import the payload & fuel for the flight

Select the instrument departure and planned approach

Import the performance numbers on the PERF INIT page

Complete the takeoff performance pages

Import the cruise and descent winds

Complete the APPROACH REF page as we get closer to the approach phase

The overall feel of the unit, combined with the firm, deliberate key presses, adds another layer of immersion. More importantly, having a physical CDU means we can operate it directly — rather than panning the camera toward the virtual CDU, zooming in, and navigating it with a mouse. This makes interacting with the FMS considerably faster and more intuitive.

This is particularly useful when ATC gives you a direct-to instruction shortly after takeoff, while you are still hand-flying the aircraft. Performing the direct-to operation on a physical CDU is much easier than interacting with the virtual CDU, as it allows you to make the necessary inputs without taking your eyes away from the Primary Flight Display.

One of the first things that stood out was the extremely low input latency. Our key presses were reflected almost instantly on both the unit’s physical display and the virtual CDU inside Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, making the two feel effectively synchronized.

We were also able to switch seamlessly between the various CDU pages, even with longer flight plans loaded into the unit. Everything shown on the virtual CDU was accurately reproduced on the hardware, including aircraft-specific options for the PMDG 737-800 we were flying. The information was presented with accurate fonts, colors, and formatting, making the physical CDU feel like a natural extension of the one inside the simulator.

Overall Thoughts

The CS 737X CDU v2 is the most premium and immersive Boeing 737 CDU we have tested. From the weight and feel of its metallic construction to the tactile resistance of the silicone keys and the accurate rendering of fonts and colors on the display, nearly every aspect of the unit contributes to an authentic experience. It's a fitting addition to any high-end home cockpit setup.

This level of construction and attention to detail comes at a price: the CS 737X CDU v2 retails for $799, which means it will likely be out of reach for many flight simmers. But if you're building a dedicated, high-end cockpit and looking for a CDU that closely replicates the experience of the real aircraft, it's an excellent addition.

articles.title: EA Adds 'Don't Delete' Message to Madden NFL 27 in Bid to Keep Players From Making Room Ahead of GTA 6
articles.description: EA has added a "don't delete" pop-up message to Madden NFL 27, and players can't help but feel the company is begging them not to make room for Grand Theft Auto 6.
articles.content:
EA has added a "don't delete" pop-up message to Madden NFL 27, and players can't help but feel the company is begging them not to make room for Grand Theft Auto 6.

Reports of the new in-game notice began cropping up over the weekend, with CharlieIntel relaying their findings online. EA doesn't explicitly mention GTA 6 in the new message, but considering the pop-up features some familiar pink-and-purple colors and sun-kissed palm trees, it's pretty easy to put two and two together.

The message encourages Madden NFL 27 users to refrain from uninstalling the game from their devices, promising that those who stick around can look forward to a new update coming Tuesday, November 17. It's a bit beside the point, but we should also mention that, at least based on early screenshots, EA's message includes a typo, writing "awating signal" instead of "awaiting signal." Newer posts suggest it was fixed pretty quickly. Whoops!

EA has added a 'Don't Delete!' message to EA Madden NFL 27 ahead of Grand Theft Auto VI's launch

The in-game ad says there's an update on Nov 17 for the title, before GTA VI https://t.co/P00NPUVveK

— CharlieIntel (@charlieINTEL) November 14, 2026

"Don't Delete!" the Madden pop-up says. "[ENCRYPTED SIGNAL] The target is locked. The crew is assembling for a high-stakes run. Await the signal from our insider on 11/17… do not leak this transmission!"

There's just no getting around it; the next week is going to be very, very weird for the gaming industry. GTA 6, a decade-in-the-making video game said to bring the biggest launch of all time, has mostly seen every other game clear the calendar just to make room for it. The atmosphere surrounding Rockstar Games' latest is something to behold, and with millions of players still turning up for live-service titles, one can wonder if any of their developers are worried about GTA 6 taking a chunk of their attention.

That at least seems to be the case for EA and Madden NFL 27. If a Vice City-themed pop-up in this year's annual football game release wasn't enough to convince you, its official X/Twitter account actually recently doubled down. A November 10 post promoting a November 18 update referenced GTA 6's massive file size by saying, "Don't let 210GB get between you and Your League."

It all seems in good fun, but fans say they can't help but feel like EA is doing everything in its power to keep players interested. Some even say it feels like the company is begging them to stay.

When one Reddit user asked what the message was related to, one user replied, "It means that EA is terrified of GTA VI's launch." Another said it felt like the pop-up was the publisher's way of saying, "'PLEASE DON'T DELETE MADDEN TO CLEAR SPACE FOR GTA. PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE!'"

articles.content:
After rumors of Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards being withdrawn from the consumer retail channel, it is pleasing to see major U.S. e-tailers like Newegg stuffed with stock today. Checking out this popular online electronics retailer, we note that there are 21 RTX 5090 SKUs available, and 11 are sold by and shipped by Newegg. Sadly, pricing remains in 3x MSRP+ territory at the time of writing. Remember, you can sift through pricing trends in our comprehensive GPU price tracking 2026 feature to see that Nvidia's Blackwell flagship was once available at its fabled sub-$2,000 price.

(Image credit: Newegg ) Despite what looks on the surface like an ample supply (but there are order limits of one per customer), prices for RTX 5090s remain extremely high. The best prices we can see at Newegg are $6,599, but this price applies only to a water-cooled Aorus model and another sold inside a Gigabyte AI BOX eGPU. They might still appeal to you, depending on your setup, though.

For a ‘standard’ air-cooled graphics card, albeit a very nice Aorus RTX 5090 Master, you’ll need to squeeze at least $6,659 out of your savings. A bonus with this card, alongside several others from the Gigabyte stables now purchasable from Newegg, is that it comes with a free motherboard. Many of these Gigabyte Aorus designs are being bundled with a full-ATX-sized X870 Aorus Elite WIFI7 AM5 motherboard, purportedly worth $319. Please note that the same motherboard is available to purchase outside this bundle for a more reasonable $249.

If you have money to burn, there are plenty of even more expensive SKUs to pick from. There are no opulent Golden Dhabab models on Newegg, sadly, but you’ll still be asked to part with $11,896 for the Asus ROG Astral GeForce RTX 5090 Edition 20 (sold by a Newegg marketplace partner). Perhaps surprisingly, given recent trending pricing news, that’s the only model above $10K, but there are still many models that are almost $10,000 from Asus, MSI, and Zotac. Even an Nvidia Founders Edition RTX 5090 refurb is priced at $8,899.

In context, these RTX 5090s are still at astronomical prices for consumer gaming PC add-in hardware. But they are now purchasable from a big retailer with fast delivery, rather than off a random scalper. It was only a month ago that rumors swirled about the RTX 5090 and the RTX 5080 being withdrawn from retail. That seemed to trigger crazy levels of price inflation, and reports of $10,000+ prices for the flagship card seemed to become the norm.

One can only hope that stock continues to flow to Newegg and other outlets, and RTX 5090 / RTX 5080 prices will settle lower as a result.

articles.title: FBI disrupts North Korean FaceStealer campaign behind $5 billion Binance hack
articles.description: US DoJ partially disrupts FaceStealer campaign that's taken $400m from victims and threatens open-source software — gov techs disrupt cloud infrastructure and find 900 videos of targeted tech workers
articles.content:
The ongoing social-engineering campaign that's reportedly taken $400 million in cryptocurrency from victims and was behind the recent Binance heist now has a name: FaceStealer. The moniker came from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ), who have announced a fight against this crime wave, starting with the seizure of associated cloud infrastructure. According to the DoJ, North Korea is behind these attacks, stealing cryptocurrency to fund its government.

The DoJ's press release on the matter is blustery, but the FBI's detailed report contains the important details. The agency's techs seized "cloud-based infrastructure," containing 900 videos of targeted victims. FaceStealer is an advanced form of spear-phishing, complete with AI deepfakes, usage of the victims' contact networks and personal information, and carefully orchestrated preparation — sometimes months in advance.

The campaign isn't likely to stop despite the setback, and has reportedly been running for at least 18 months, a timeline that matches up with documented instances of similar intrusion attempts. The largest heist attributed to FaceStealer is the recent Binance hack that saw thieves make out the proverbial door with over $5 billion (most of it thankfully frozen and/or recovered), but far from the only one.

The FBI attributes about $400m in stolen cryptocurrency to the campaign, and importantly, also notes that the hackers have repeatedly tried to sneak into open-source software, chiefly Javascript/NPM modules and Rust crates. Despite not being mentioned by name, one example hack is almost certainly the Axios compromise from March 2026. The Node/Javascript library sees about 100 million downloads a week, and temporarily contained a remote-access tool — thankfully for only a few hours.

Jason Sayayman, the Axios developer in question, got hooked by an attacker posing as a legitimate company interested in hiring him. The malfeasants replicated the CEO's persona, created a Slack workspace with legitimate-looking channels, then invited him to a Teams meeting with multiple "people."

This modus operandi is what the FBI warns about. According to the bureau, FaceStealers start by getting access to a person's communication application(s), then lifting all previous conversations, contact lists, and, most importantly, stealthily recording video of them and/or their contacts. The footage and information will then be used to catch the actual targeted victim, who'll often be sent offers for jobs or investment opportunities.

The victim will eventually be invited to a Zoom or Teams meeting that's actually hosted on an attacker-controlled server, with a typo-squatted domain like "uu01webzoom.us" or "teams.livemeet.us". The meeting will often have deepfaked AI participants and/or previous meeting recordings playing, granting the event an air of legitimacy — particularly because conversations leading up to this point will contain real information and context.

At some point, though, there will be some sort of "technical problem," and the victim will be prompted to install an "update" or software to fix the problem, which is loaded with malware. From there, the attackers have free rein over the victim's computer and data, and will siphon off browser sessions, CI/CD passwords, and all manners of access credentials to eventually get access to cryptocurrency wallets — or just use this information to find a juicier target, like the poor Binance developer through which Binance's hot wallets were broken into.

The FBI says that the above scenario may play out in multiple cycles until the attackers reach their intended target, collecting loads of precious video and information along the way to make the final strike much more convincing.

articles.title: 357 detailed CPU die shots spanning 1971 to 2024 crammed into a new gallery
articles.description: A CPU enthusiast has put together an eye-popping visual database containing crystal clear detailed die shots of 357 legendary, and some lesser-known, processors.
articles.content:
A CPU enthusiast has put together an eye-popping visual database containing crystal-clear, detailed die shots of 357 legendary and some lesser-known processors. At sheets. works/data-viz/cpu-dies, you will find a sortable, searchable, and filterable gallery featuring the outstanding, freely shared die shots from the likes of Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars, John McMaster, and Fritzchens Fritz. Find one or two of your favorites, and peer into the details to enjoy a nostalgic technological trip down memory lane. That’s what I did.

(Image credit: sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies ) The unnamed collator of this gallery might not have contributed any die shots, but has still done an admirable job putting these macrographs and micrographs together in this way. Beneath a brief introduction that credits the skilled photographers who share these images for free, you can glide through the 357-photo collection.

By default, the die shot gallery gives you the gallery view, ordered by the oldest silicon first. Those browsing the gallery can instantly switch to a True Scale gallery view, too, which provides some physical sizing context. The next view option for the gallery is a table, where you can see processor maker, year, die dimensions, and photo license at a glance, but it sacrifices visual impact by showing just tiny thumbnails.

sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies Navigating the gallery is also quick and intuitive thanks to a built-in search function. Using this, it was easy to display only 486 CPU s, for example. For your information, there are 17 486 CPU variants in this gallery with samples produced by AMD, Cyrix, IBM, TI, UMC, VLSI, and Intel of course. You can click any of the thumbnails to jump to a larger view with notes of the design, as well as photographer details/credits. Though that click zooms in the image considerably, I found that a right-click – open image in new tab - was needed to enjoy the die shot’s full visual splendor.

It would be great to see the database/gallery maintained with the latest shareable die shots from the various contributors. Also, it could be improved by fully populating details such as the die area, which is not always present. Some more searchable and sortable fields, such as transistor count, might also make this resource more satisfying.

For my personal nostalgia, I enjoyed seeing CPUs like the Motorola 68000 and the AMD Athlon XP up close. Surprisingly, some eras, including the Intel Ivy Bridge and Haswell generations, seemed underrepresented, though.

articles.title: Xbox at 25: My Memories From Across Xbox’s Entire (and Quite Incredible) History
articles.description: I’ve been lucky enough to have a front-row seat for most of the Xbox’s 25 years, covering the high highs and low lows of Microsoft’s pivot into the living room. It’s been quite a ride since November 15, 2001, and I wanted to mark the occasion by sharing some of my biggest memories with you. And, lik
articles.content:
The first day of my career was October 1, 2002. I’d been lucky enough to get hired by Official Xbox Magazine. The fledgling Xbox console was not quite a year old, and when I got settled in on the staff, it quickly became clear that Xbox was really about one thing above all else: Halo. I remember being surprised in my first days on the job by what would happen every single day, like clockwork, at 5pm: consoles and TVs would get turned on, Halo would get fired up, and we’d all play a round or two of Capture the Flag on Blood Gulch before we all went home. Fun and friendly banter ensued. Halo was baked into the Xbox’s DNA from the very start.

It is one of my very first of many thousands of great Xbox memories. I’ve been lucky enough to have a front-row seat for most of the Xbox’s 25 years, covering the high highs and low lows of Microsoft’s pivot into the living room. It’s been quite a ride since November 15, 2001, and I wanted to mark the occasion by sharing some of my biggest memories with you. And, like everything else with Xbox, it started with Halo.

Thank goodness for Combat Evolved, in fact, because most of the rest of that first year of Xbox history was pretty bleak. Lots of C++ spaghetti was thrown at the wall, and most of it didn’t stick. Oh, don’t get me wrong – there were moments! Steel Battalion, Capcom’s batshit-insane mech vertical tank simulator that cost $200 and came with its own custom 40-button controller and foot pedals was quite simply amazing as both a game and piece of hardware and would never get made today. Meanwhile, The Elder Scrolls 3: Morrowind was the beginning of Xbox becoming a Western-RPG powerhouse. But first-party hadn’t really found its footing yet, as it published stuff like the now-infamous Blinx: The Time Sweeper.

But thanks to Combat Evolved carrying the Xbox through its first trip around the sun, things got really interesting in Year Two. It turns out I joined the magazine at just the right time! Halo: Combat Evolved was the biggest very real reason to buy the console in its first year, but its critical second year was defined by three things: Xbox Live, Tom Clancy games, and BioWare.

Year Two

Xbox Live was a massive swing that connected for a home run. Back then, high-speed internet was far from ubiquitous. In fact, dial-up 56k modems still dominated the American online infrastructure. But Microsoft put a big bet on broadband by putting an Ethernet port into every Xbox. In the first year, that port only got used for Halo LAN (er, System Link) parties, but then, on the one-year anniversary of the system on November 15, 2002, Xbox Live launched. And it was a loud launch in the very best of ways. MechAssault brought an action-first take on MechWarrior to the console audience – including an excellent multiplayer suite – while a faithful port of the PC’s outstanding military FPS Tom Clancy’s Ghost Recon was a perfect fit for the new online service. And all of it was buttery smooth and almost entirely free of latency on account of everyone being on a high-speed connection. Plus, every Xbox Live kit came with a chat headset, and in those earliest days, people actually used them! Party Chat didn’t exist yet, so everyone talked to each other, and trolls were few and far between on account of the service having a $50 per year buy-in.

A mere two days later, a second, wholly original (albeit single-player-only) Tom Clancy release dropped exclusively on Xbox: Splinter Cell. PlayStation had Solid Snake, but the young Xbox had the sardonic and effortlessly cool Sam Fisher (voiced to perfection by the irreplaceable Michael Ironside). Incredible real-time lighting, super-fun spy gadgets, memorable setpieces, and stellar stealth gameplay all combined to create an instant hit for Xbox – and one that also served as a technical showpiece for the console’s potent graphical capabilities.

The Tom Clancy brand becoming synonymous with Xbox would only continue in 2003. The Tom Clancy brand becoming synonymous with Xbox would only continue in 2003, when yet another Tom Clancy gem, Rainbow Six 3, hit Xbox that holiday and did some truly awesome stuff. For one, it looked and sounded great. That was a common thread running through all of the early Clancy games on Xbox: great visuals and sublime Dolby 5.1 surround sound. But more than that, its campaign was augmented by a compelling new feature: commanding your AI squadmates with your voice. Remember that chat headset that was bundled in with every Xbox Live Starter Kit a year earlier? The brilliant designers at Ubisoft Montreal had put it to good use, allowing you to shout things like, “Go! Go! Go!” when all of your guys were stacked up at a door and ready to breach. I sounded like an absolute lunatic doing this in the middle of the OXM office as I reviewed the game, but did it add to the fun? Unequivocally, yes. And then that same chat headset got put to great use for its original purpose: online multiplayer. Rainbow Six 3 dominated Xbox Live; it was arguably the online service’s first killer app. Xbox Live programming director Larry “Major Nelson” Hryb used to regularly post the top 10 most-played games on Xbox Live, and Rainbow Six was firmly entrenched in the top spot for months after its release (until November of 2004; you can probably guess why, but we’ll get to that…).

But 2003 saw far more than just one significant release for Xbox. That summer gave us one of the five best original Xbox games ever – a truly special release that doubled as one of the best Star Wars games ever made and tripled as one of the best RPGs ever made. And I had the tremendous pleasure of reviewing it. It was, of course, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, an epic tale set thousands of years before the original film trilogy that let you fully embrace either the Light Side or Dark Side of the Force. I opted for the latter, mostly because no game I’d ever played had fully supported evil choices. But KOTOR absolutely did, allowing me to double-cross people I’d made deals with and generally just be terrible. It was glorious, and it legitimized RPGs on the Xbox. I still remember driving 45 minutes from the OXM office to Skywalker Ranch to get the review build installed on my Xbox debug kit. I had no idea what a ride I was about to go on, and to this day KOTOR remains either my 1a or 1b favorite RPG of all time, along with the very next Xbox-exclusive game the KOTOR development team at BioWare would make, which I’ll talk more about later.

Grand Theft Auto 3 and Vice City also came to Xbox in 2003 as part of the GTA Double Pack, as did Max Payne 2 and one of Xbox Live’s first big multiplayer hits, the class-based first-person shooter Return to Castle Wolfenstein: Tides of War. The much-hyped first-party exclusive Brute Force dropped that year, too, and though it couldn’t quite live up to its “The Next Halo?” headline we’d put on it on the cover of OXM ahead of its release, it was nevertheless pretty good, though it failed to take off. But Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge, a console continuation of a previous PC game, very much did, becoming another Xbox Live hit. So did the golf action of Links 2004 and the tennis competition found in Top Spin – two pillars of the short-lived XSN program. Voodoo Vince, meanwhile, was a really good platformer even if it didn’t sell all that well. But you know what did? Project Gotham Racing 2, a semi-realistic racer that deftly straddled the line between sim and arcade and proved to be a huge success. First party was finally starting to find its footing beyond Halo.

Halo Freakin’ 2

Xbox’s third year built on the impressive momentum of the previous one. A murderer’s row of killer games hit the console in 2004. You already know the big one, but let’s not forget about the rest. In fact, the 2004 lineup begins with another top-five original-Xbox GOAT, Ninja Gaiden. Designer Tomonobu Itagaki (may he rest in peace ) and Team Ninja followed its Dead or Alive 3 day-one Xbox launch title with a revival of the 1980’s arcade and NES classic, translated gloriously into a 3D fast-action challenge of your wits and skill. My colleague Mitchell Saltzman, a connoisseur of the genre, called Ninja Gaiden the best pure action game ever made – and he did so 20 years after Ninja Gaiden’s release. And he’s absolutely right. We had a playable demo of Ninja Gaiden on the OXM demo disc prior to its release, and we got enthusiastic letters about it for months on end. That demo probably sold tens of thousands of copies of that game, and it was a point of pride and a privilege for us to be able to be the vehicle for introducing so many Xbox gamers to it.

Just a few weeks later, Splinter Cell returned with Pandora Tomorrow, delivering another excellent stealth campaign. But that’s not what Splinter Cell’s first sequel is best remembered for. That honor goes to another reason you absolutely had to pony up the $50 annual subscription for Xbox Live if you hadn’t already: the wholly original, wildly innovative Spies vs. Mercenaries multiplayer mode. In it, two Sam Fisher-like Spies – playing from the same third-person perspective as the single-player campaign – faced off against two first-person-viewing, heavily armed Mercs as they battled over objectives. Spies were nonlethal with one notable exception: if they could sneak up behind the Merc and grab him around the neck from behind, not only could they break said neck to take them out, but the mic chat would suddenly open up, allowing the Spy to vocally taunt the Merc before making the kill. It was genius stuff that’s still revered today.

I’ve already written extensively about The Chronicles of Riddick: Escape from Butcher Bay and shared my memories of when developer Starbreeze first brought it to the OXM office, but hoo-boy, what a masterpiece this was. All of a sudden, licensed games weren’t terrible by default. I’d go so far as to say a lot of games based on an existing IP owe a debt of gratitude to Riddick.

Which brings me to Fable. Is it on the short list of best Xbox games ever? Admittedly, not quite – and I say that as the person who reviewed it for OXM and gave it a very strong 8.9 out of 10. But it did successfully birth a franchise, and it was a great game. It had the unfortunate burden of having to live up to series co-creator Peter Molyneux’s boasts and promises – most notably how Fable would have such advanced systems that you could plant an acorn early in the game, and by the end of the campaign it would grow into a full tree (you couldn’t). But this was a world full of charm and humor and some really high-quality action-adventuring. And it was a hit!

And then there was Halo 2. Where to even begin? It was probably the most fun I’ve ever had in my career covering a single game. The buildup to November 9, 2004 was unlike anything I’ve experienced as a gamer or as a media professional both before and since. The hype was truly unprecedented – everyone was fired up for it. In the pre-social media era where monoculture was still alive, Halo 2 had everyone’s attention. I’ve never been more excited for a first hands-on with a game than I was the first time I laid hands on Halo 2 back at E3 2004. The year prior, Bungie showed the now-infamous single-player demo – but nobody in the media got to play it.

In 2004, however, my first taste of Halo 2 came from a single-flag CTF match on the Zanzibar map during E3. Dual-wielding weapons, boarding vehicles, the new graphics, the new weapons – it was all in there! Remember, we’d been playing Halo 1 multiplayer at OXM every day; we’d never stopped. So to say I was excited for the first new Halo of any kind since the original would be a colossal understatement. These behind-closed-doors multiplayer sessions were by appointment only, and as you can imagine, they were booked solid throughout the entire week of E3. But inevitably there were no-shows here and there, and I was able to sneak my way back in for a couple more

articles.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, finds evidence of DRAM collusion plausible after 500% price surge
articles.description: The judge characterized the three companies as "hawks flying in formation" when it came to their business decisions.
articles.content:
Judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed. According to the decision, the defendants’ argument that the legal action is just “a rerun” of the same antitrust case filed against the industry in 2018 was rejected as the plaintiffs have established that there’s some new evidence suggesting that there was collusion between the big three memory chip manufacturers.

Go deeper with TH Premium: Memory

(Image credit: SK Hynix) AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supply

Samsung debuts three next-generation memory technologies for AI data centers

The future of DRAM: From DDR5 to future ICs

High-bandwidth memory roadmap

Inside the history of DRAM price-fixing lawsuits

Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is. Judge Wise disagreed with this characterization, though, saying that what they are accused of goes beyond that. “Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation — an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.”

The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year. One of the events they cited included the “simultaneous DRAM production cuts” from October 2022 to April 2023, which was quickly followed by a “coordinated pivot to HBM.” They also said that the three companies announced the winding down of DDR4 production in a span of three months and have failed to expand the production capacity “despite these extraordinary prices — the single most powerful supply signal the DRAM industry has ever produced.”

Other factors that the suing parties brought to the table include the introduction of stringent customer vetting procedures in response to the shortage, the refusal to sign long-term contracts for DRAM customers, Micron’s decision to shut down Crucial (its consumer memory brand), multiple statements projecting the shortage, as well as their involvement in previous price-fixing scandals.

The big three memory chip makers argued that all of these are logical business moves so that they can maximize their revenue during a period of great demand and that they are “consistent with [their own] independent self-interest.” They also said that they appear to have similar behaviors because they’re in a highly concentrated market, and that they’re all “reacting to the same market pressures,” thus it would make sense for them to have a similar response.

Despite their rebuttals, the judge decided that the case is plausible enough to move forward. This isn’t a judgment, though — both sides would still have to show their evidence and speak their arguments before the court before getting a decision. Because of this, the three companies are given until December 7 to respond to the original complaint with the case management conference, which will determine the administrative matters on the case, set for January 2027.

articles.title: DuckDB has an answer to “bloated” database messages
articles.description: Older database protocols were built before big data. Some still send results row by row, repeating details like column names The post DuckDB has an answer to “bloated” database messages appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Older database protocols were built before big data. Some still send results row by row, repeating details like column names and types with every row. The result, says DuckLabs product team lead Guillermo Sánchez Dionis, is “quite a bloated message.” That overhead adds up when you’re moving large query results.

DuckDB’s answer is Quack, an HTTP-based protocol that streams query results in batches of column data as DuckDB produces them. It was previewed in May and was released in October as part of DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS.

On this latest episode of The New Stack podcast, recorded at DuckLabs headquarters in Amsterdam, Sánchez Dionis explains how that design lets developers start working with results while a query is still running.

A database protocol is a formal set of rules and message formats that dictates how a client application communicates with a database server. It acts as a specialized language that lets a software application securely send SQL queries, receive structured data tables, and manage transactions over a network. It handles connection and authentication, query packaging, data serialization, and error management.

But according to Sánchez Dionis, most protocols were designed pre-big data for other types of systems, with serialized rows rather than columns. They also add a lot of unnecessary data, he says, like column types and column names per row.

“It becomes quite a bloated message. That already makes the protocol not only not good for analytical systems, but it’s also quite heavy,” he contends. As protocols evolved for analytical systems, they did start using columns, but “they were still doing things like serializing one value at a time and other things that are really not efficient. Modern systems are trying to converge on using vectorized execution to be able to serialize more values at a time and trying to use more efficient representations of columnar data formats to send over the wire.”

All while the Quack protocol, he says, is aiming for a different, highly efficient approach.

Quack is DuckDB’s HTTP-based client/server protocol, with its first production release shipping in DuckDB 2.0.0 on Oct. 21. Not only does this signal Quack moving out of the preview stage, but the protocol now offers certain developer-friendly features:

The CONNECT statement allows developers to attach to and query a remote Quack server via standard SQL commands.

The new -serve CLI argument instantly starts a Quack server instance from the command line, and -connect connects to one.

Multiple clients can write to the same database concurrently, with transactions handled under DuckDB’s multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) isolation.

“Quack uses DuckDB’s data chunks — which is our columnar representation of data. We also serialize in a very efficient manner because we are a vectorized engine. We also make sure that we send the results in a streaming fashion,” Sánchez Dionis explains.

“One of the most important things is tightly coupling the engine. Once you start producing results, instead of waiting for the query execution to end and then serializing all of the results at once, you serialize and send results as they are emitted by the engine. Therefore, the client can keep consuming results without having to stop the engine.”

For developers, he says, that means they don’t have to do anything.

“I think the biggest advantage that you will see is you will have a very small memory footprint”

“You run a query from the comfort of your laptop, and you just get streaming results back. I think the biggest advantage that you will see is you will have a very small memory footprint,” he says. “What’s cool about Quack is that you install and load it wherever you are. You can also create another client on the [same] laptop with the Quack extension, and they will communicate with each other.”

Then, the scale of how many DuckDB servers is up to you and your team. And the overhead of running it on that server is next to none, Sánchez Dionis continues, as it’s Quack’s biggest efficiency gain yet.

More Quack improvements are expected in upcoming DuckDB 2.0 patch releases, as the DuckLabs team looks to build stability on the server side.

articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Opus 5.5: Same scores at almost 4x the cost
articles.description: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9 and said it beats Claude Opus 5.5 in almost every capability the The post Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Opus 5.5: Same scores at almost 4x the cost appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9 and said it beats Claude Opus 5.5 in almost every capability the company measured. In the same announcement, it recommended starting with Opus for most coding and knowledge tasks, calling it its “strongest daily driver.” I wanted to find out why a company would steer people away from its best model, and whether the cheaper one really is enough.

…why a company would steer people away from its best model, and whether the cheaper one really is enough.

On Anthropic’s coding benchmarks, Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% at Xhigh effort on FrontierCode 2.0, compared with 45.5% for Opus 5.5 at Max. Anthropic also reports that Fable scored 45.3% at High effort at roughly half the cost per task of that Opus run. On FrontierSWE v2, the company reports 69.9% for Fable and 62.3% for Opus. Fable’s standard API rates are twice Opus’s: $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, versus $4 and $20.

Twice the price should make a meaningful difference, so I gave both models three coding and agent jobs and measured how well they did, how many tokens they used, what they cost, and how long they took. My tests are much smaller than Anthropic’s benchmarks and can’t prove or disprove those scores. 

The tests

I ran each model once per test through Anthropic’s API at default settings, with no turn cap. Anthropic’s API defaults on Fable and Opus aren’t equal. Fable 5.2 runs at high effort, and Opus 5.5 runs at medium, so these results show what a developer gets without tuning anything. I used a script to grade each answer the model gave for each test. The dollar figures are estimated API costs based on reported token usage. Anthropic prices uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, and output separately.

Here are the tests I ran:

Cron scheduler: I gave each model a written spec for code that runs when the next scheduled job runs, then sent a change request. I used a hidden suite of 50 tests to grade the final code.

Invoicing repo fix: Each model worked as an agent in a small invoicing library with interacting bugs in rounding, discounts, tax, and shipping. The library also had one wrong test that the model should report but not edit.

Incident investigation: Each model used a terminal to find the cause of a payments outage from logs, metrics, and deployment records. The data included decoy deploys and servers with wrong clocks.

The models tied with perfect scores on the first version of every test, so I made each test harder and reran it twice.

Cron scheduler

This test checks whether a model can turn a detailed spec into correct code and then absorb a change without breaking it. Here’s what differed between the versions.

Version 1: The spec covered standard cron schedules, such as every 15 minutes or weekdays at 9 a.m.

Version 2: I added rules like “the weekday nearest the 15th” and “the last Friday of the month,” and the change request reversed how two fields combine.

Version 3: The code had to handle time zones and daylight saving time by hand, without Python’s time zone library.

Both models scored 50/50 on all three versions. The difference was in how much work each one did to get there. Fable 5.2 wrote two to three times as much reasoning as Opus 5.5 on every version. The extra reasoning did not raise Fable’s score on any of the three versions.

The extra reasoning did not raise Fable’s score on any of the three versions.

Across the three scheduler versions, Opus matched Fable’s scores in 358 seconds versus 661 and cost an estimated $0.99 versus $3.29.

The numbers:

Version 1

Fable 5.2: 2 turns, 14,471 in, 18,732 out (11,122 reasoning), $0.87, 170 s.

Opus 5.5: 2 turns, 8,055 in, 9,431 out (3,846 reasoning), $0.22, 80 s.

Version 2

Fable 5.2: 2 turns, 20,215 in, 23,990 out (14,627 reasoning), $1.12, 226 s.

Opus 5.5: 2 turns, 14,090 in, 15,991 out (6,695 reasoning), $0.38, 131 s.

Version 3

Fable 5.2: 2 turns, 21,121 in, 28,254 out (17,452 reasoning), $1.30, 265 s.

Opus 5.5: 2 turns, 12,651 in, 17,205 out (6,533 reasoning), $0.39, 147 s.

Invoicing repo fix

This bug hunt is similar to the work agents do for developers daily. Here’s how I adjusted the tests with each round:

Version 1: The library had bugs in rounding, discounts, tax, and shipping. It also had one wrong test.

Version 2: I added buy-two-get-one promotions, weight-based shipping, and refunds, each with its own bugs.

Version 3: I added currency conversion and invoice numbering, again with bugs.

This test produced the widest gap in cost and time between the two models. Both models scored 50 of 50 on all three versions, fixing the bugs the grader covered and reporting the wrong test without editing it. Opus 5.5 used fewer reasoning tokens on every version. It finished each version in under a minute, while Fable 5.2 took about one minute and 46 seconds to just under four minutes and cost eight times as much across the three.

On these runs, Fable’s extra reasoning didn’t improve its score.

The numbers:

Version 1

Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 17,585 in, 11,511 out (5,909 reasoning), $0.58, 106 s.

Opus 5.5: 4 turns, 10,585 in, 2,975 out (519 reasoning), $0.09, 28 s.

Version 2

Fable 5.2: 6 turns, 88,697 in, 25,980 out (11,820 reasoning), $1.39, 223 s.

Opus 5.5: 4 turns, 13,938 in, 4,457 out (777 reasoning), $0.13, 39 s.

Version 3

Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 29,660 in, 24,020 out (14,022 reasoning), $1.18, 214 s.

Opus 5.5: 5 turns, 24,208 in, 6,013 out (1,178 reasoning), $0.17, 51 s.

Incident investigation

This test rewards careful digging more than fast coding, so I expected it to favor Fable 5.2.

Here are the changes I made for each test version.

Version 1: The outage data had decoy deploys and one server whose clock ran seven minutes slow.

Version 2: I added a clock that was corrected partway through the incident, retried requests, a compressed log file, and duplicated log lines.

Version 3: I added a server that logged in Chicago time and an unrelated error spike inside the incident window.

Both models scored perfectly (50 out of 50) across all three versions. Fable 5.2 took fewer turns in every version, 9 to 11 versus Opus 5.5’s 12 to 14. Across all three versions, Fable’s estimated cost was $2.54 versus Opus’s $0.91.

The numbers:

Version 1

Fable 5.2: 9 turns, 155,925 in, 14,309 out (8,638 reasoning), $0.94, 143 s.

Opus 5.5: 12 turns, 111,618 in, 7,405 out (2,801 reasoning), $0.25, 73 s.

Version 2

Fable 5.2: 11 turns, 168,913 in, 9,416 out (3,551 reasoning), $0.68, 105 s.

Opus 5.5: 13 turns, 188,846 in, 7,218 out (2,518 reasoning), $0.32, 82 s.

Version 3

Fable 5.2: 10 turns, 205,601 in, 11,887 out (4,474 reasoning), $0.92, 127 s.

Opus 5.5: 14 turns, 253,958 in, 7,598 out (2,041 reasoning), $0.34, 70 s.

Results

Total tokens in / out 722,188 / 168,099 637,949 / 78,293

Total estimated cost (sum of displayed estimates) $8.98 $2.29

Total time 1,579 s 701 s

The scores were identical across all nine runs per model. Fable 5.2 cost almost four times as much and took more than twice as long.

What do I think?

These tests give me a reason to start with Opus 5.5 for work like this. It matched Fable 5.2’s score and finished faster on every version, at about a quarter of the estimated cost overall.

That doesn’t make Fable 5.2 a bad model. My tests were hard but short. Anthropic recommends Fable for more open-ended technical work. I tested each model at its API default, so the comparison leaves open how much of the gap comes from the different effort settings.

I’d start with Opus 5.5 and move up to Fable 5.2 only when Opus stops producing ideal results.

articles.title: 3D printing dev’s free tool unlocks curved printing along all three axes
articles.description: PancakeSlicer is a self-hostable non-planar 3D printing slicer that might finally make non-planar slicing more accessible to the masses.
articles.content:
Alpaca Engineering posted a YouTube video yesterday showcasing his self-hostable non-planar slicer. He explains that most non-planar 3D printing — printing across all three axes, rather than in 2D horizontal layers — demonstrations are usually for research purposes, for demonstration and experimentation, with no easy way for most 3D printer owners to try out non-planar 3D printing. His project, named PancakeSlicer, aims to fix this by making his non-planar slicing algorithm as easy to implement as existing slicing workflows, even improving upon it with 3D printer management features.

Alpaca Engineering explains that every few months, a non-planar 3D printing demonstration goes viral, but is rarely adopted practically by most 3D printer owners. Most non-planar experiments are for research, with half-abandoned GitHub projects. He further explains that non-planar isn’t widely adopted not because there aren’t any general-purpose non-planar slicers, but because it’s not accessible and easily implemented in a familiar workflow, with 3D printer owners spoiled by modern workflows and not needing to manually run G-code directly from an SD card.

Commercially available 3D printers are also not optimized for non-planar 3D printing. The challenge with printing at various angles is the clearance angle needed to bring a print head up and down without crashing into its own print. The slicer uses 3D models of various print heads from different 3D printer models to know how to slice the object to avoid collisions, thus having limited support; but Alpaca Engineering has listed a large number of supported 3D printers from Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Voron, and many others. The varying shapes of the print heads also mean different printers will have different capabilities, with some managing less angle and curvature than others.

Alpaca Engineering also has great animations and practical demonstrations of the different slicing algorithms in the slicer, including how the algorithm slices the object for non-planar printing. We highly suggest you watch the video if you’re interested, as his animations explain non-planar slicing intuitively.

One of the best features of this slicer is its self-hosting features. Users can host the slicer from a desktop, NAS, or a home server and access it with a web UI, allowing multiple users to send print jobs from any device. It also has 3D printer management features, applying different profiles to different printer brands, unifying the experience without hopping from one slicer to another to operate multiple 3D printers — this is even available to Bambu Lab users, replacing Bambu Studio and Bambu Connect in LAN-only mode. The slicer can also manage two slice jobs at the same time in case other users happen to be slicing at the same time.

While PancakeSlicer isn’t the first to implement self-hosted 3D printer management features, it certainly levels up his initial goal of making non-planar slicing as easy to access as most modern workflows. We hope to see how more people can experiment with non-planar 3D printing, contribute their findings, and rapidly improve upon it as a genuinely practical slicing method.

articles.title: Enthusiast builds a working 486 DX2 retro PC on a breadboard in just 16 days, immediately runs Doom
articles.description: An app engineer has showcased his homemade breadboard 486DX2 PC running Doom, put together in just over two weeks.
articles.content:
An app engineer has showcased his homemade breadboard 486 DX2 PC running Doom. The intricate explosion-of-wires system build appears to have taken just 16 days, with the first appearance of the legendary Intel CPU on @nagakurage’s timeline on October 24, and a video demo of some fragging in Doom published on November 9. Moreover, the Tokyo-based app engineer behind the project also developed and made a bezelicious ‘CRT monitor’ to go with the homemade early-90s-era gaming beast.

はじめてDOOMで遊びます、自作のi486 PCで https://t.co/feosWgd6de November 9, 2026

This project’s first signs of life were seen towards the end of October. On October 24, @nagakurage showcased the legendary Intel i486 DX2 CPU that he had acquired. It was the sought-after DX2 66 model, which meant it ran at a blistering 66 MHz internally, and 33 MHz externally (2x multiplier). On the other side of this gray made-in-Malaysia chip, you can see its 168 pins, which look incredibly tree-trunk-like by today’s standards.

The enthusiast next bought a Colorlight i9 v7.2 FPGA board to attach the CPU to and to cover chipset duties. We know this is a breadboard PC, but there are limits… Every pin of the 486 CPU appears to have been connected separately to an experimental ‘socket’ made using a baseboard.

i486 CPU実験用ソケット完成低クロックで動かなければ基盤発注する https://t.co/cXCnvPtkQ5 October 24, 2026

A significant milestone was reached on October 26, when the finished form of the breadboard system started to come into view, and the dev managed to get the CPU to blink an LED using x86 code. RAM was added on October 31, and tweaked to be error-free. Then, on November 3, the enthusiast managed to add microSD storage to the system. That same day @nagakurage enjoyed seeing the breadboard 486 boot FreeDOS 1.3 for the first time [machine translation].

The app developer then took a 3D printing diversion and used his Bambu Lab A1 mini to output the parts necessary for a custom CRT-style enclosure. This was designed by Claude and was assembled with a 5-inch 800×480 Elecrow Raspberry Pi panel inside.

Finally, on November 9, @nagakurage showcased his breadboard PC and era-matching design beige-shelled monitor side-by-side and powered up. The seminal shooter looked smooth enough on the vintage 1992 silicon, as it should do.

Going forward, the enthusiast wants to refine this breadboard-based project and make it fully PC-98 compatible, in line with the dominant NEC PC-9800 series in Japan in the early 90s.

In April this year, we reported on another retro computing enthusiast and their breadboard-based Intel 386 system build.
