articles.title: Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer
articles.description: AI agents have had a URL problem for a while. When an agent needs current information but has no search The post Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
AI agents have had a URL problem for a while. When an agent needs current information but has no search tool, it often makes up the web address it thinks the answer lives at. It might guess something like docs.example.com/v4.2/auth, try to load it, and get a “page not found” error because the page doesn’t exist. Then it either keeps guessing or falls back on outdated information from its training.

“Live web search gives AI agents fresh pages. Deciding which ones to trust over your own data is still a ranking problem.”

Infrastructure providers have noticed. In October, InfoQ reported that Cloudflare opened a beta Web Search API in its AI Gateway. Agents can call several search providers through one interface and get live results back with source links, logging, and access controls attached. Cloudflare’s reasoning was refreshingly direct: Without search, agents tend to guess.

This is a welcome change, and live search will probably be a default agent tool within a year, but it solves only the finding part of the problem. Once fresh pages are in front of an agent, something still has to decide which of those pages, and which of your own documents, the agent should actually rely on. That decision lives in your retrieval layer.

The problem: two pools of evidence, one context window

An agent working inside a company rarely answers from the web alone. It also has the data that makes it useful to that company: product catalogs, documentation, contracts, support history, account records,s and permissions. With web search wired in, every step of a task can now pull from two very different pools.

Web results Internal data

Freshness Often hours or days old Can be months out of date without anyone noticing

Quality Uneven: official docs next to forum threads Curated, but written for a past state of the product

Structure Mostly unstructured text Mix of text, metadata and structured records

Authority Has to be inferred from the source Known, but rarely stored as a field

Access control Public Per customer, region, contract or role

The agent has to reconcile these, often several times within one task. And the questions it needs answered are ones a search API was never built to handle. When yesterday’s vendor changelog contradicts an internal knowledge base article from last spring, which one wins? Does this result apply to this customer’s version and region? Is the agent even allowed to show it?

Those are ranking and filtering decisions. They depend on your data and business rules, so you have to make them where both are available.

Why concatenating results breaks in production

The simplest integration is to run a web search, run an internal search, append one list to the other, and let the model sort it out. It may work well at first, but once it’s running against growing data and traffic, it tends to fail in a few predictable ways:

Conflicts go unresolved. The model sees two confident sources that disagree and has no signal for which is newer or more authoritative, so it picks one or blends them into an answer that matches neither. 

Staleness hides. A 3-month-old knowledge base article that matches the user’s wording almost exactly will beat a 4-day-old changelog on similarity alone. Nothing in the embedding says the article is out of date. 

Permissions are applied too late. If access rules run after retrieval, restricted content may already be in the prompt. If they run crudely, useful results get dropped along with sensitive ones. 

Cost and latency compound. A person runs one search and reads the results. An agent can trigger a dozen or more retrieval calls in a single task as it plans, checks, and refines. Sending every candidate to the model on every call adds up quickly, and more context doesn’t reliably produce better answers.

A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does. 

“A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does.”

Clarm, a Y Combinator company that builds sales and support agents for open-source software companies, hit this early. Its founder, Marcus Storm-Mollard, said the team realized “search, not generation, was the real problem to solve.” Generating an answer was the easy part. Finding the right information to ground it in was the hard part, which is why Clarm runs text search, vector similarity, and structured filters through a single query instead of stitching separate stores together.

What changes when agents search across sources

When agents combine live web results with internal data, they need to account for different retrieval methods, metadata, permissions, and ranking signals. Four design considerations stand out.

1. Retrieve across methods in one query 

Keyword matching catches exact product names, error codes, and version strings, which embeddings are notoriously bad at. Vector search catches paraphrases and intent. Structured filters enforce hard constraints like customer, version, and entitlement.  

Within a single indexed collection, hybrid retrieval can combine keyword matching, vector similarity, and structured filters. That does not, by itself, fuse results from an external web search API with results from an internal index. The two-source integration requires a separate design decision.

select * from evidence where
({targetHits: 200}nearestNeighbor(embedding, q) or userQuery())
and visibility contains "customer"
and product_version contains "4.2"

The broader lesson is that retrieval systems need to handle lexical matching, semantic similarity, and filtering together. These requirements matter regardless of the search platform chosen. Perplexity hit this wall when it set out to build search in-house for its answer engine. Its CEO, Aravind Srinivas, has summed up the company’s approach as “first solve search, then solve everything else.” But when the team evaluated existing tools, it found that vector databases couldn’t reliably support even simple Boolean filters, while traditional search backends offered only primitive semantic ranking. It needed lexical retrieval, semantic retrieval, and filtering in one engine, at consumer scale, and chose Vespa to build it.

2. Rank on more than similarity

Relevance to the query is only one signal. Agents also need to weigh freshness, source authority, and business rules together: official documentation over forum threads, last week’s changelog over last year’s wiki page, the customer’s contracted version over the latest release.

Multiphase ranking is a practical way to do this. A cheap first phase scores thousands of candidates on a blend of signals, and a more expensive learned model reorders the few that remain: 

rank-profile agent_evidence {
inputs {
query(q) tensor (x[384])
}
rank-properties {
freshness(published_at).maxAge: 7776000
}
first-phase {
expression: bm25(body) + closeness(field, embedding) + 0.5 * freshness(published_at) + attribute(source_authority)
}
second-phase {
rerank-count: 100
expression: xgboost("evidence-ranker.json")
}
}

The important part isn’t the specific weights. It’s that freshness and authority are explicit, inspectable inputs to the score, not something you hope the model infers from the text. (The maxAge setting controls how quickly freshness decays; here it’s 90 days.)

“The important part isn’t the specific weights. It’s that freshness and authority are explicit, inspectable inputs to the score, not something you hope the model infers from the text.”

Metal AI, which builds an intelligence platform for private equity firms, runs into this with due diligence questionnaires. Firms answer thousands of them from investors, and a model can’t freely generate the answers. They have to come from a bank of responses that legal has already approved, and that bank changes over time and lives in documents and spreadsheets. Similarity alone could easily surface an approved answer that’s been replaced. So Metal indexes the answer bank with recency in mind and ranks freshness alongside semantic similarity, so the agent pulls the current approved answer, not just the closest match. 

3. Treat web results as candidates, not answers

Web search and internal retrieval often return separate result sets, each with its own relevance signals. Simply passing both sets to the model leaves it to reconcile differences in freshness, authority, and relevance. 

A more deliberate approach is to evaluate evidence from both sources against a consistent set of criteria before selecting what goes into the prompt. Vespa’s flexible ranking capabilities can support this approach, but the implementation depends on how the external results are integrated into the retrieval pipeline.

Depending on provider terms and system constraints, teams might index permitted external content into a shared search collection or retrieve from separate systems and apply a subsequent fusion or reranking step. There is no universal fusion method. Each option has trade-offs in latency, freshness, score comparability, and operational complexity.

4. Hold up at agent call volume

This isn’t a hypothetical load pattern. At Metal, AI agents handle 95% of retrieval, not people. When someone asks for a portfolio company’s EBITDA, an agent decides which entity types to query (documents, companies, metrics, activities), applies recency and workflow filters, runs the query, and then keeps going, paginating or pulling related entities until it has enough context to answer. Clarm sees something similar from the other direction: developers working alongside its agents send thousands of queries a day, in sessions that have run as long as 22 hours.

“They need the precision and controls of expert search, delivered with the low latency and high throughput of consumer search.”

Every one of those calls sits on the critical path to the agent’s answer. Retrieval and ranking need to stay predictable under that load, which favors running inference where the data already lives instead of shipping large candidate sets across the network to a separate ranking service. Every network hop you remove is latency you get back on every call, multiplied by every step of the task. Jon Bratseth, Vespa’s CEO, describes this as the central engineering challenge with agents: They need the precision and controls of expert search, delivered with the low latency and high throughput of consumer search.

A worked example: the support agent and the changelog

Here’s a scenario most support teams will recognize. A customer upgrades a payments SDK from 4.1 to 4.2, their checkout integration stops working, and they open a ticket. 

The agent does what you’d want and searches the web first. It finds the SDK’s changelog from four days ago, which deprecates the authentication call the integration relies on, and a forum thread where another developer posted a workaround. Then it searches internally, returning a March knowledge base article that still tells customers to use the old call, the customer’s account record showing they’re on 4.2, and a restricted engineering ticket about the same bug.

Handed to the model as one long list, this is a trap. The knowledge base article matches the customer’s wording almost exactly, so it ranks well on similarity. The forum workaround reads confidently. The engineering ticket contains notes the customer should never see. 

When the retrieval layer is doing its job, both sets of evidence go through the same pipeline. In this example, the team uses a shared collection: web results are indexed into Vespa as short-lived documents alongside internal data, retrieved with one query and scored by rank profiles aligned with the same business rules:

For this ticket, that means:

The visibility filter excludes the internal ticket at query time, so it never reaches the prompt.

The version filter keeps only material that applies to the library version on the customer’s account.

articles.title: DuckLake 1.1 solves the absurd complexity of data lakes at AI scale
articles.description: How much simpler could a data lakehouse get if an ordinary SQL database kept track of its files? That’s the The post DuckLake 1.1 solves the absurd complexity of data lakes at AI scale appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
How much simpler could a data lakehouse get if an ordinary SQL database kept track of its files? That’s the question in this episode of The New Stack podcast.

DuckLake is an open-source table lakehouse format created by Amsterdam-based DuckLabs that acts as a traffic cop for data management by storing table metadata inside a standard SQL database, rather than scattering manifest files across object storage. Unlike traditional table formats, DuckLake treats lakehouse metadata as a relational database problem. These advanced data lake features, served by Parquet files and SQL databases, reduce the traditional lakehouse complexity.

In October, DuckLake 1.1 launched alongside DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS. The New Stack sat down with Pedro Holanda, lead DuckLake developer and principal engineer at DuckLabs at their Amsterdam headquarters, to talk about the launch. Holanda has contributed to the DuckDB open-source project since it was an early research prototype, and shares the full evolution of DuckLake to our conversation.

“These lakehouse formats exist so people can exchange their database systems without having to do migrations,” Holanda tells The New Stack. Because of the complexity, “you need a database system to keep track of which table has its last version.”

DuckLake applies decades of research, Holanda says, in order to reduce files and therefore complexity at a time of rapid data growth, taking advantage of how everyone who uses database systems is familiar with SQL and how schemas work.

“The simplicity is the way you fetch your data,” Holanda says of DuckLake. “You’re going to issue queries somewhere. The server is going to answer these questions back, and you know exactly which Parquet files you have to read. So the Parquet files don’t change. Just the catalog.”

Maintainers of your data lake often have many maintenance tasks to perform. If you end up with many files, he says, DuckLake lets you glue them into one file to reduce the number of requests. This can also be done across multiple snapshots, further reducing the number of files. It also solves the “small files problem” in streaming data lakes and lakehouses by using inlining and flushing.

Whereas for traditional data lakes, across multiple data sources being inserted at a time, “you end up with so many files, so when you have to query it, you’re going to have to traverse a bunch of metadata files just to figure out which Parquet files you need to read, and then you’re going to have a bunch of Parquet files to read as well,” Holanda says, slowing everything down and frustrating the developer.

DuckLake is known to be fast, simple to use, and not requiring massive server clusters to run. Part of that comes from Parquet being very similar to DuckDB storage: both are columnar and organized in row groups, which keeps the massaging step to a minimum.

“One thing that we realized when we were building DuckLake is that, ‘Hey, we have a database system now, we have a catalog; what if we do this radical idea of storing data on tables?'” he says. “With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.”

“With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.”

During Amazon’s Q3 earnings call in late October, CEO Andy Jassy called out the complexity of moving data between data stores and analytics engines, especially as AWS customers’ data generation continues to increase. Amazon is famous for dogfooding, and Jassy pointed to DuckDB’s solution to this complexity as a reason for its DuckLabs acquisition.

“With our acquisition of DuckLabs, DuckDB will become the universal SQL dialect of AWS storage and analytics, simplifying data processing with a modern analytics engine that is fast, simple to use and ubiquitous, and where customers will be able to write SQL queries once and then execute using any AWS analytics service,” Jassy said. “For the first time in analytics, customers will have zero migration or portability costs between query engines. This is a big deal, and you can imagine how it will also help agents do efficient querying as well.”

DuckDB and DuckLake remain free and open source under the MIT license, overseen by the independent DuckDB Foundation.

Overall, this recent DuckLake release pairs new features with more than 200 bug fixes for quality and stability, and it runs natively in DuckDB.

articles.title: Anthropic wants you to build on Claude. There’s a catch.
articles.description: Anthropic wants developers to build businesses on Claude, but its expansion into enterprise software is raising concerns among founders that The post Anthropic wants you to build on Claude. There’s a catch. appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Anthropic wants developers to build businesses on Claude, but its expansion into enterprise software is raising concerns among founders that the company supplying their models could eventually become their biggest competitor.

A nervous warning to wrappers

Gerald Zingraf, president and COO of GlacierGrid, raised the concern on LinkedIn following Anthropic’s Tuesday expansion of Claude’s enterprise lineup, comparing its strategy to Amazon’s private-label business.

“Makes me nervous for wrappers and pure SaaS companies,” Zingraf writes, drawing on his experience selling products he designed through Amazon before watching the retailer introduce competing products.

“Makes me nervous for wrappers and pure SaaS companies,”

His concern is that Anthropic can see which third-party integrations customers use most frequently and potentially draw on that information when deciding which capabilities to build itself.

“Anthropic has the same view,” he argues, although he offers no evidence that the company uses integration data to identify competitors or inform its product roadmap. For some developers, the risk is no longer hypothetical.

When partners become rivals

Scott Stevenson, CEO of legal AI startup Spellbook, described what happened when Anthropic moved into his company’s market in a November 2 interview with Forbes.

Spellbook uses Claude models for everything from reviewing contracts and suggesting revisions to automating legal workflows. Stevenson recalls Anthropic employees assuring him the company had no plans to compete directly in legal software, before Anthropic launched Claude for Legal, which includes contract-review capabilities that overlap with Spellbook’s business.

“Anthropic has been a great partner, but it made us realize that they are a massive company and two parts of the org can have conflicting mandates,”

“Anthropic has been a great partner, but it made us realize that they are a massive company and two parts of the org can have conflicting mandates,” Stevenson said in the interview. “Ultimately this is inevitable.”

Spellbook hasn’t abandoned Claude. Anthropic still features the startup as a customer, reporting roughly 530,000 monthly contract reviews performed by its Claude-powered agents, while Stevenson also appears in Anthropic’s October 28 announcement of legal artifacts.

The relationship illustrates a difficult position for developers whose products depend on frontier models. Spellbook still benefits from Anthropic’s technology, even as Anthropic develops applications aimed at some of the same customers. Nothing in Stevenson’s account establishes that Anthropic used Spellbook’s proprietary information to develop its legal offering.

When the platform ships your product

Tech founder and Dalton Mills CEO Todd Saunders made a similar argument in a March 10 post on X, following Anthropic’s introduction of Claude Code Review.

“Anthropic is the new Amazon,”

“Anthropic is the new Amazon,” Saunders writes, warning developers building on Claude’s SDK that the company could observe application usage and eventually incorporate competing functionality into Claude.

The company’s November 10 announcement introduced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, while previewing Claude Meetings. Expanded interactive connectors also let partners embed applications directly inside Claude, including software from Adobe and Atlassian.

What the policies leave unsaid

Anthropic has access to information about how customers interact with third-party apps and services, something the company acknowledges in its privacy policy, effective September 10, 2026. What isn’t clear is whether Anthropic looks at which integrations are most popular when deciding what to build next.

The rules are different for business customers. Under Anthropic’s commercial terms, customers retain rights to their inputs and own their outputs, while Anthropic agrees not to use their content to train its models. Its commercial privacy documentation also says feedback data excludes content pulled through connectors, including local and remote MCP servers, unless users paste it directly into a conversation.

Neither document settles how Anthropic uses aggregated integration data.

The tradeoff developers accept

The company is still encouraging developers to build on Claude. It’s just that access to its growing enterprise customer base comes with a tradeoff, since Anthropic controls the interface and can introduce competing features without consulting the developers who depend on it.

For now, Anthropic is asking developers to trust it as both a technology provider and a business partner, even as it moves into markets those same developers are trying to build businesses in. Whether that relationship remains sustainable may depend less on what Anthropic promises today than on what it decides to ship next.

The New Stack has contacted Anthropic for comment and has not received a response.

articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. GPT-6 Astra: A lower list price didn’t mean a lower bill
articles.description: Anthropic is positioning its new model, Claude Fable 5.2, for demanding coding and technical work. Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 on The post Claude Fable 5.2 vs. GPT-6 Astra: A lower list price didn’t mean a lower bill appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Anthropic is positioning its new model, Claude Fable 5.2, for demanding coding and technical work. Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 on Nov. 9 and reported higher scores than OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on two coding benchmarks. Fable 5.2 also has lower standard API rates.

Anthropic’s launch benchmarks put Fable 5.2 ahead of Astra, 49.1% to 42.8% on FrontierCode 2.0 and 69.9% to 65.5% on FrontierSWE v2. Fable’s 49.1% came at X high effort. At High, its default on the Claude API, it scored 45.3%. Benchmark leads don’t always carry over to real work.

The cost side is less simple than the price list. Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and AI companies bill by them. At standard API rates, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra in September at standard API rates of $10 per million uncached input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. “The price per task is what matters,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said at Astra’s launch. Both APIs charge for reasoning tokens as output and have separate rates for cached input.

In my experience, Anthropic’s models have used more tokens than OpenAI’s. I put this positioning to the test and ran Fable 5.2 against Astra on tasks that simulate real developer work.

The tests

I ran both models on the same three tasks, once each, through each vendor’s API at default settings. Each test is worth 50 points, and I used a script to grade all the answers. Here are the tests:

Bug fix: I planted 10 bugs in a 2,600-line billing codebase and wrote a support ticket describing 10 customer complaints. The ticket’s guesses about the causes are wrong, two of the codebase’s own tests are wrong, and one bug only shows up after another is fixed.

Code review: I planted 45 defects in its VAT ID checks for 27 countries, its IBAN rules, its European Central Bank payment calendar, and its date formats for 50 locales in an EU invoicing package. The models had to prove each defect with an input the code gets wrong and identify the correct answer. Flagging false alarms cost the models points.

Code writing: The model wrote the same helpers from scratch, including VAT ID validation for 27 countries, IBAN checks for 34 countries, the payment calendar, and long dates.

Bug fix

Fable 5.2 and Astra fixed all 10 bugs and passed all 50 hidden checks, both in 12 turns (the matching number of turns surprised me).

The difference is in how much each model spent to get there. Fable 5.2 used more than 17,000 reasoning tokens, and Astra used 819 (wow). Astra passed the checks in about two minutes at an estimated cost of 98 cents. Fable 5.2 took more than five minutes and cost an estimated $2.51.

The numbers:

Fable 5.2: 12 turns, 696,863 in, 36,135 out (17,387 reasoning), $2.51, 326 s.

Astra: 12 turns, 231,854 in, 6,823 out (819 reasoning), $0.98, 122 s.

Code review

This is the only test where the scores differ. Fable 5.2 scored 49, and Astra scored 45. Fable 5.2 proved 44 of the 45 defects and raised no false alarms across 71 findings. Astra proved 41 and incorrectly classified one Spanish ID as valid. Astra missed defects in check-digit rules for Spain, Ireland, and Luxembourg. Both models missed the same Spanish defect: two swapped letters in a 23-letter lookup table.

Fable 5.2’s thoroughness came at a price. It cost more than six times what Astra did and took more than four times as long. If your code handles invoices (or simple approvals), one validation rule the review misses can get real invoices rejected, so Fable 5.2’s four extra points may be worth the higher price. For a routine review, Astra found 91% of the defects for 16% of the cost. Each model ran once, so a four-point gap could shift on another run.

The numbers:

Fable 5.2: 26 turns, 2,207,564 in, 103,240 out (77,641 reasoning), $6.05, 993 s.

Astra: 12 turns, 192,018 in, 8,664 out (4,307 reasoning), $0.95, 227 s.

Code writing

Both models scored 50 of 50. Each one wrote working checks for 27 countries’ VAT IDs and 34 countries’ IBANs with no libraries to lean on. Neither model had trouble here. Both passed all the checks in one run.

Astra took 23 turns, almost as many as Fable 5.2’s 24. Fable 5.2 still cost 2.3 times as much and took 1.7 times as long for the same score. In this run, the extra tokens didn’t raise the score.

The numbers:

Fable 5.2: 24 turns, 1,495,712 in, 87,542 out (47,458 reasoning), $4.83, 838 s.

Astra: 23 turns, 460,271 in, 24,007 out (9,328 reasoning), $2.06, 483 s.

Results

Test Claude Fable 5.2 GPT-6 Astra

Bug fix (of 50) 50 50

Code review (of 50) 49 45

Code writing (out of 50) 50 50

Total tokens in / out 4,400,139 / 226,917 884,143 / 39,494

Estimated cost $13.39 $3.99

Total time 2,157 s 832 s

Fable 5.2 led on code review and tied Astra on the other two tasks. Across the two tied tasks, its estimated API cost was 2.4 times Astra’s ($7.34 vs. $3.04), and it took 1.9 times as long (1,164 vs. 605 seconds).

What do I think?

For tasks like these, I’d start with Astra. It matched Fable 5.2’s scores on bug fixing and code writing at about 41% of the estimated cost, and it finished all three tasks faster. I’d consider Fable 5.2 for a careful code review, where it found three more defects in this test. Both models missed defects.

Fable 5.2’s standard token rates are lower, but it used about five times as many tokens as Astra across these three runs. Brockman’s point about price per task held up here.

articles.title: Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about
articles.description: Collabora and Nextcloud pitch alternatives as education customers weigh the cost of losing free services
articles.content:
The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.

The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news.

As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like. Or, for that matter, other US tech giants.

Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners.

The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks.

A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill.

Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud."

A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't."

The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly."

Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure. Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted.

Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty.

Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register: "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure.

"Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy."

Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®

articles.title: Breaking Down Theo's Shock Moment in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 and the Mystery of His Father With Actor Tyroe Muhafidin
articles.description: A spoiler-filled The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 interview with Theo actor Tyroe Muhafidin.
articles.content:
Warning! Spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 Episodes 1-4 follow.

If you’re caught up with The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, you’ll have watched Season 3, Episode 4 and were probably left reeling by a shock character death that leaves the elves in a spot of bother going into the final stretch.

During the first four episodes of Season 3, we see Theo, played by Tyroe Muhafidin, tempted by Sauron into becoming a Nazgnagôl. Nazgnagôl are men who wear one of Sauron’s Rings of Power, but still retain something of their humanity. That is, they are not fully Nazgûl, or Ringwraiths, as we know of the beings in the Third Age of J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth. They are, at this stage, Ring Servants.

Theo, last seen as a hopeful child of the Southlands and friend of hero elf Arondir, is now older and full of hate after five years of Númenórean oppression. Sauron sees something in him, something special, and offers Theo a gift. In Episode 2, appropriately called The Gift of Men, Sauron performs a dark ritual that lets Theo “meet” his mysterious father, or at least that’s what we think is happening here (with Sauron, you never really know!).

This is a callback to a scene in Season 1 where a young Theo encounters The Hilt, a broken sword-hilt forged during the First Age. It had been left hidden in a barn where Theo discovers it, and we see Theo’s blood drip into the Hilt, somehow feeding its regeneration. Clearly, Theo had some dark power inside him, although it was left unaddressed, sparking many fan theories over recent years.

In Season 3, Sauron notices the dark mark left on Theo’s arm after his interaction with The Hilt and immediately raises an eyebrow. Who was Theo’s father, really? During the ritual, Sauron uses the power of necromancy to communicate with the dead in the Unseen World. Sauron listens to the words of the dead, and tells Theo his father was named Fäldred, Son of Hammethreg. Theo asks, “Who are you, father?” The response, in Black Speech, is “Gorthmundur.” Sauron tells Theo this was a “Noble House of old, the sworn stewards of Mordor blessed with… certain powers.”

These powers, it seems, were passed down to Theo. “There is a reason you were drawn to that hilt, and it to you,” Sauron continues, before suggesting that Theo might have become ruler of the Southlands had his mother not “hidden the truth.” Theo responds to say his mother told him his father left. Sauron disputes this, before issuing a revelation that sends Theo spiralling: his mother murdered his father over what he had become.

Sauron, ever the opportunist, offers Theo a Ring of Power. He tells him that he has the power within him to become “a conqueror, a sorcerer, a king.” The downcast Theo accepts the gift.

Fast forward to Episode 4, and one of two shock deaths that punctuate this first block of The Rings of Power Season 3. Theo, now in full Nazgnagôl gear and spurred on by Sauron, murders his friend Arondir during the escape from Gundabad. It’s a shocking twist that cements Theo’s descent into darkness, and marks the end of the road for one of the mighty heroes of The Rings of Power.

In the interview below, I ask Tyroe Muhafidin about Theo’s journey in these first four episodes, what it’s like to play a Nazgnagôl, and where the murder of Arondir leaves The Rings of Power. And yes, we get into the question of Theo’s parentage. Was Sauron telling him the truth about his father?

IGN: The first question is an obvious one: how does it feel to be playing a Nazgnagôl?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It was crazy. The costume automatically gives you a sense of such great strength and power. The biggest thing for me was, as soon as I put on those gauntlets there was an automatic transforming moment for me where you could just feel the power through your body. And it's interesting because I went from playing basically a helpless child to some godlike being. So it was a real jump and I had to do a lot of work in terms of my physicality and trying to look powerful and strong, which was something so new to me because I've always been scrawny and helpless. So yeah, it was a challenge, but I think I got there in the end, and I'm super, super grateful that I've got a chance to be something so iconic and to play something so iconic.

IGN: What is your understanding of what Nazgnagôl are, as it was explained to you?

Tyroe Muhafidin: So a Nazgûl directly translates to Ringwraith, whereas Nazgnagôl directly translates to Ring Servant. At this point in time when we've just put the ring on, we're not quite wraiths yet. We are still human men with autonomy over their body and can make their own decisions. We're just a lot stronger now. We've got a lot of power and a lot of dark power.

An important thing to know is at the beginning of this season, the One Ring hasn't yet been made. So these rings are yet to be binded completely to Sauron's will, where we are not now complete, I guess, his minions. We still have autonomy over who we are. That was the fun thing to play in this season, the gradual descent into more and more madness and more and more evil and darkness. But at this point in time, we get to very much still be people, just very strong people, I guess.

IGN: There's a really interesting scene where Sauron reveals Theo's parentage to him. What's your understanding of who Theo's father is? Sauron is suggesting at that moment that Theo has an innate power as a result of his parentage, but it's left ambiguous. And Sauron looks emotional even as he's talking to Theo about this. I almost was thinking he almost looks at him as his own son in some ways. So what's your read on that? What can you tell us about what all that means?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It's revealed that his father was the head of a few dark sorcerers and he sided with the dark side a long time ago, alongside his peers and the other Southlanders who sided with Sauron. And so there's that kind of information that's brought out.

But I think the big thing for Theo is when Sauron says his mother killed him when she found out. And I think that moment for me, and I think for Theo as a whole, it kind of sends a spin in the works of, what is Sauron really doing here and what is he trying to accomplish? Is he just trying to say words to make Theo happy, trying to build this broken boy up? Because he can see something for sure. And I don't think Theo really realizes. But I think there was always a dark side to Theo and maybe it was inherited, but that relationship to the Hilt was always something that stuck with him.

And I think maybe when he got a taste of that darkness in the Hilt, maybe it was the first time he kind of felt the presence of his father, and maybe that's why it was so addictive, that feeling to him. So I think this season we find out a little bit more of where he comes from.

But I think the biggest thing is, how much of it is the truth? What is Sauron saying that is manipulation and deceit and what is the truth? Which I think is kind of the fun dynamic of those scenes, is you feel like you're finding out a lot, but are you really?

IGN: There is a big moment in Episode 4 where Theo kills Arondir, a character who's been in the series from the beginning. When you first found out you'd be doing that, what was your reaction?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It was interesting. I was excited because I was like, "Oh, this is some juicy stuff to get into." But I think the moment I got the script, I found out and I was really excited because it was going to be some really cool stuff. When I read it all, it all became very real for me. And it was like, "Wow, this is a big task. This is super daunting." And there were months of intense anxiety coming up to this moment. But yeah, I guess I was just super excited, but anxious at the same time. And I feel like I knew at some point something big like this was going to happen. So I think it was just a matter of being prepared for it and trying to service Ismail [Cruz Córdova, who plays Arondir] as well, the best I possibly could.

IGN: What do you think the character death means for the show at that point and the story it's telling, but also for Theo? Do you see it as this is a moment that we see a tipping point in him that the audience is like, "Okay, yes, he has really gone too far."

Tyroe Muhafidin: In terms of the show, it's a moment of no-one is safe and there's no mercy from the dark side. And this war is very much real. The most talented and bravest of your warriors will go down. And that's kind of, I think, setting the premise for the rest of the war that's going to go on.

I think for Theo specifically, it definitely was that tipping point where his decision is made and his destiny is decided. And I think he realizes this afterwards as well, and whether he agrees with that decision he's made or not, he's made that decision.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 episodes 1-4 are out now on Prime Video. Check back with IGN after Episodes 5 and 6 are released this week for more.

articles.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
articles.description: Accessing banned content is as easy as whipping out a thesaurus, Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee hears
articles.content:
Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say.

A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters.

Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms.

"Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said.

"I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable.

"So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently."

McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not.

"If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added.

"And we know your algorithm would."

Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too.

Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal.

She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly.

There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs.

"So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content."

Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories.

With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process.

Success of user reports trails away

As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially.

Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent.

Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures.

The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly.

Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limbo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests.

Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report, it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny.

Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment.

The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force.

England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference " to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves.

Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms.

She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.'

"In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered.

"So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

articles.title: FAA blames ground stop on faulty copper wiring
articles.description: Safety reasons and unspecified communications issue cited
articles.content:
The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevented the takeoff of flights in US airspace for around five hours, creating chaos for travelers and airports. The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded.

In a press conference Saturday, Transportation Secretary Duffy attributed the FAA ground stop to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade. Duffy said it has yet to be determined whether the issue was incompetence or a faulty router.

In a statement provided to The Register on Saturday, a spokesperson for L3Harris said, “L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

The stop was issued on Friday around the middle of the day ET.

"The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement on Friday. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them."

A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone at the time said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement.

The FAA ATCSCC advisory halted departing flights and said international flights would be dealt with individually.

The notice said, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis."

Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now."

An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage."

The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. ®

Updated at 0039 UTC Sunday UTC with the administration's explanation for the stop.

Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop.

Updated to add at 2353 UTC

CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.”

Updated to add at 2340 UTC

Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

articles.title: Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again)
articles.description: Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did. Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intell
articles.content:
Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did.

Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants, rings, and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long.

Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps, collaborative software, or your cloud backup solutions, have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are all now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game.

Tech companies want us to accept a reality where one person’s privacy choices (or lack thereof) means you suddenly need to be an expert in consumer tech who understands the capabilities of many devices on the market, how they work, how and if they signal when they’re recording, and what platforms they do or do not connect to. They believe these ambient surveillance devices that work in the background and are designed to look as normal as possible are the future, while they also expect the owners of these devices to use them responsibly and to notify those around them of their capabilities to act within whatever laws their states may have. 

This is not reasonable, nor how consent works in any practical sense.

Let’s break this down by looking at some of the biggest players currently in the game: Apple and Amazon, who have two different takes on transcribing audio throughout the day, as well as Meta and Google, who both have slapped AI and cameras onto eyeglasses. 

How to Think About the Technical Promises Companies Make

Ask Apple about privacy concerns and they’ll point to a white paper that explains all the technical barriers between them as a company and the data generated by the watch. Ask Meta and they’ll talk about all the ways you can customize the privacy controls or how certain details, like faces, may be blurred out when you interact with Meta AI through the glasses (but not during standard recording). Google does this too. Amazon will also talk about how you’re always in control, and no audio is stored (though it’ll also let you enable Amazon store integration, so your conversations can directly result in ads for products). And so on across all the companies making these products.

Some of these solutions do a better job than others at cutting out potential law enforcement or company access to this data. There will be a time to dive into these details more deeply, but the technical privacy promises these companies focus on only cover the consumer and user of the device. They ignore every bystander you interact with and their inability to actually opt out. There is no technical protection for you as a non-user of these devices, the person who finds yourself captured by them. 

Still, we hope to look deeper into the technical differences between this category of devices soon.

There Must Be Some Laws to Consider, Right?

With something like Apple’s Audio Intelligence and Amazon’s Bee devices, it may be best to treat them similar to an always-recording microphone, even if companies try to claim there’s “technically” no audio recording. These tools still often use a microphone to capture raw audio from conversations and convert it into summaries or transcripts before discarding the audio. Google's blog post notes that it has  whole responsible use part of their Terms of Service where users have to agree not to record others without permission or in sensitive places. 

But it’s not just the question of the legality from the point of view of the user. Law enforcement will eventually try to compel access to the data that these products create (either real-time audio or the summaries and transcripts they create). And while some products, like Apple’s Audio Intelligence, are engineered to make that difficult, not every product will be. We know from history that when data exists, governments will do everything they can to access it. There’s no reason to think something would change today.

No Tech and Legal Solutions Will Reduce Social Issues

There is a problem humming along in the background that is impossible to address with technical or legal solutions. If secretly documenting conversations becomes the norm, it makes every private conversation less spontaneous and open. It breaks a longstanding social norm that you will not record and document every conversation with friends, family, colleagues, or strangers. 

The companies that make these sorts of products like to claim they’re no different from tools we already have. You can easily record everything right now with a phone or a camera. Heck, you can do so with a camcorder or cassette recorder if you want. And you can transcribe conversations with pen and paper, too. But those are actionable steps we take that both require effort from the user, and are clear to others around us. This new wave of passive surveillance tech is designed to encourage continuous monitoring and hide its use. 

Even taken at face value, none of these products can understand the complex social context we all navigate every day. We intrinsically know there are different social agreements we all make when we’re standing on a street corner, at a protest, in a bathroom, at a doctor’s office, at the gym, or in a restaurant. Taking notes in a meeting at work is completely normal. Getting a summary of a conversation with your best friend about their divorce is not. Always-on monitoring of our conversations is an unacceptable burden on our conversational privacy. 

Google seems to all but admit this problem in a conversation with CNN when it described the company’s experiments with a notification system that would alert people’s phones when someone was recording nearby: 

“And just alerting bystanders doesn’t do much to help, [Juston Payne, senior director of product management at Google] said. “It can actually be weirdly disempowering to you in that you’re like, ‘What am I meant to do now?’” he said.”

What We Can Do About It

It’s easy to buy into the tech company line that these products are inevitable, but we’ve seen so many vaporware products over the years that we should take those claims of success with a grain of salt. We’ve seen entire product categories come and go within just a few years, and if the public doesn’t want this stuff, the tech companies will have to throw in the towel. 

Of course, that doesn’t mean we all just have to sit around and hope that’s what happens. For its part, Apple launched its Audio Intelligence features in beta specifically to get feedback, and we think it’s worth taking the time to fill out their feedback forms (or in the Feedback Assistant app if you’re in the beta) and let them know what you think.

Products from the likes of Meta, Google, Amazon, and others might be harder to push back on, but politely and clearly engaging with those who use them in ways that make you uncomfortable is a good place to start. And if you see abusive videos on social networks where these sorts of products are used, report them. If you find these products useful for yourself, make it clear to those around you when you’re using them, and only do so with consent and in social moments where it makes sense to do so.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

articles.title: Anthropic now lets you self-host Claude Managed Agents. The catch? 8 hours to act if it flags a safety risk in the software
articles.description: Anthropic has unveiled a self-hosted version of its platform for building and running AI agents. Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents, as The post Anthropic now lets you self-host Claude Managed Agents. The catch? 8 hours to act if it flags a safety risk in the software appeared first on The New Stack
articles.content:
Anthropic has unveiled a self-hosted version of its platform for building and running AI agents.

Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents, as it’s aptly called, is available now in private beta. Customers host both the server that coordinates the agents and the sandboxes where the agents run their tools, either in their own cloud account or in an on-premises data center. Credentials and session histories stay on their infrastructure, while requests to Claude go to the inference provider they configure.

While the benefits of self-hosting are evident, particularly for companies handling sensitive data, the accompanying license comes with a number of notable caveats that may give some customers pause — this includes strict deadlines for responding to safety notices, limits on which models customers can use, and rules against preventing certain types of data from being sent to Anthropic.

Claude’s road to self-hosting

Back in April, Anthropic debuted Claude Managed Agents, a hosted service for building and running AI agents. The following month, the company launched self-hosted sandboxes, which let customers run agents’ tools on their own infrastructure while Anthropic continued to run the Claude Managed Agents server.

With self-hosted Claude Managed Agents now in the mix, customers can run that server themselves, too, and store session histories in their own database.

In a blog post marking the launch, Anthropic says agents are taking on more consequential engineering tasks, including repairing failed builds, checking releases and deciding which alerts need attention. That work can require access to sensitive systems, such as private code repositories and internal build and release systems.

“For agents with that level of access, some teams want the whole service in their own environment, not just the sandbox.”

“They run unattended on your code and need access to your internal systems,” the company writes. “For agents with that level of access, some teams want the whole service in their own environment, not just the sandbox. Until now, that meant building the platform themselves.”

Several companies have done exactly that. Spotify developed Honk, which runs Claude through the Agent SDK inside Spotify’s own harness. The company deploys Honk in Kubernetes pods in its cloud environment, giving it access to its internal CI systems so it can run builds and verify its code changes.

Anthropic’s new offering packages much of that work into a product. Customers run Anthropic’s server and the sandbox workers in their own cloud or data centre, with PostgreSQL if they want to retain session histories across restarts, while their developers use the same core APIs as they do with the hosted service. The local server can send requests to Claude through Anthropic’s API, a cloud provider such as Amazon Bedrock or Microsoft Foundry, or the company’s own gateway.

The devil in the detail: 8 hours to act

While Anthropic’s formal announcement emphasizes why companies might want to host the service themselves, digging into the details of the license reveals how much control Anthropic retains over the software once it’s deployed.

For starters, Anthropic ships the server as a proprietary binary that customers can’t modify, meaning that they can’t patch or customize the server code themselves. They can route requests through their own gateway, but only to Claude models. The license also bars models from other developers unless Anthropic expressly permits them, and the public inference docs list only Claude models.

Among the most notable terms of the license is how little time customers have to act on Anthropic’s safety notices. If the company flags a safety, security or misuse risk in writing, customers have just eight hours to disable the affected feature or roll back the version across every deployment. They also have one business day from delivery to install a designated safety update.

§5.3 Eight hours to roll back or disable

Patrick Moorhead, founder and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, says the eight-hour deadline is tighter than the time most large enterprises typically allow to make production changes.

“Self-hosted usually means the customer owns the change window,” Moorhead tells The New Stack. “This license flips that.”

“Self-hosted usually means the customer owns the change window. This license flips that.”

Even within the Claude model lineup itself, access can vary. The license says Anthropic can decide, on safety grounds, that some or all of a licensee’s customers should access certain Claude models only through Anthropic’s hosted service.

§5.6 Anthropic can reserve models for hosted access

Moreover, the license bars customers from blocking or altering what it calls “usage signals,” the observability data the software may send to Anthropic. The company can use this data to measure how much the software is used and to monitor compliance with the agreement.

“The idea is that if you build an agent that is breaking the law or causing harm you cannot stop us [the model lab] from figuring that out and doing anything about it.”

Jason Andersen, also an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, says the telemetry clause and the separate requirement to maintain safeguards Anthropic specifies are broadly in line with how cloud vendors would try to prevent misuse.

“The idea is that if you build an agent that is breaking the law or causing harm you cannot stop us [the model lab] from figuring that out and doing anything about it,” Andersen tells The New Stack.

§5.9 Customers can’t block usage signals

The security backdrop

In July, Anthropic disclosed that Claude models had gained unauthorized access to real computer systems during cybersecurity evaluations. That same month, OpenAI had disclosed that models undergoing internal tests had bypassed isolation controls and breached systems at Hugging Face.

While a model provider can address a problem on its side, an agent running on a customer’s servers may keep operating. And so the customer may also need to take action to contain the problem.

“I do think that this is Anthropic putting more teeth around safety to limit their exposure which is effectively what a license does,” Andersen says. “It does not really change the risk of the technology it makes or those who use it to make agents.”

How enterprise buyers might respond

The long and short of all this is that Managed Agents now comes in three forms: fully-hosted by Anthropic, hosted by Anthropic with customer-run sandboxes, and now fully self-hosted.

Whether that third option works for buyers depends on what they need from self-hosting in the first place. Moorhead expects regulated buyers to push back on both the rollback deadline and the telemetry terms.

“It’s workable for companies already comfortable running Claude as a cloud service, and they’ll treat this as a cloud service that happens to sit in their data center,” he says. “For banks, government and sovereign buyers, expect procurement and legal to push back on sections 5.3 [safety rollback] and 5.9 [usage signals].”

Andersen, for his part, says the terms are “a reasonable ask” for enterprises, and doubts they’ll slow adoption overall, given that buyers who need full control over their agents would likely be looking elsewhere already.

“If you needed that level of control on your agents, you would likely consider a more independent, possibly open-weight solution,” he says.

articles.title: Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer
articles.description: Forensic report finds Blackwell's fingerprint in DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group models
articles.content:
US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer.

Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models."

"This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," said DePue in a social media post. "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model."

It doesn't sound that insane. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed from revelations that he had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who, in 2023, founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International. That company is reportedly under investigation by US authorities for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

Huang's departure coincides with a renewed push to tighten US chip export controls. House Speaker Mike Johnson supports the idea. And there are at least four bills awaiting consideration that aim to limit China's access to leading edge AI tech: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, Match Act, and the Cloud Security Act.

On Monday, US Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) cited Jensen Huang's "relationship with a suspected Chinese spy" as a justification for passing the AI Overwatch Act, which would codify the Trump administration's existing chip export controls. The Trump administration on Thursday said it's not sure whether Alice Huang was a spy, an allegation denied by Beijing and currently under investigation by the FBI.

Whatever the case, the current rules clearly are not working. Only a few weeks ago, Lava, an Israel-based security company, said it had found "32 Nvidia B300 GPUs, part of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra generation, through publicly exposed monitoring endpoints with IP addresses geolocated to China."

These GPUs, Lava noted, are subject to US export controls [PDF]. The security biz said its findings followed from the exposure of monitoring systems intended for internal infrastructure management that were publicly exposed.

How DePue reached his conclusion

The analysis published through DePue's consultancy, "Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs," takes a different approach: analyzing the published weights of various models from Chinese AI labs.

As described in the report, model weights – the parameters that change in relation to training data – must be initialized with some value. One method for doing so involves a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox. The algorithm starts with a seed value that produces the same set of initial values whenever it's run.

Using PyTorch, initialization can be done by creating multiple GPU threads that work in parallel, with the help of Nvidia's cuRAND library. And because this process is not truly random, it's possible to select a chip and a seed value, generate the initial weights for that hardware and compare that pattern to a model's published weights.

"I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models," said DePue. "In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models – including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3 – were initialized on Nvidia Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in Nvidia's flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems."

Noting that this is the first time MiniMax and Ant Group have been publicly linked to usage of Nvidia's Blackwell, he also cited several limitations to his approach. One is that usage of Blackwell GPUs doesn't prove where the GPUs were located, so it's possible some of these Chinese labs used this hardware through US providers – a loophole the Cloud Security Act aims to close.

DePue's report includes initial seed values that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Nvidia's Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, for those who wish to attempt to reproduce the results. DuPue claims that multiple senior researchers, both independent and inside frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, have confirmed the result.

Coincidentally, OpenAI and Anthropic have each complained about Chinese labs copying their models through distillation, a pastime also noted by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. ®

articles.title: This year’s bug count just passed 100K
articles.description: ‘We don’t have a security problem anymore. We have a data problem now’
articles.content:
Chalk up a new record for vulns. The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI.

“It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register. “The thing that almost scares the bejesus out of me is while 100K sounds like a lot, in a couple years we're going to say, remember when it was only 100K?”

As of the time of our interview, about 4 pm UTC on Friday, VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs, he said. Microsoft alone added 1,094 security flaws to the total count on Tuesday, following 1,474 vulnerabilities the month before.

“There's no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we're seeing.” All the major CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) - these are the organizations authorized by the CVE program to assign unique identifiers to security vulnerabilities - like VulnCheck, Microsoft, Oracle, GitHub, and other large enterprise IT vendors “are just screaming into the atmosphere right now,” Bressers said. “It’s AI.”

Meanwhile, the percentage of these bugs that are exploited in the wild remains relatively consistent. About 1.4 percent (1,363) of the CVEs published this year have been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

“But obviously, as the number of CVEs grows, [1 percent] of 1,000 is a lot different than [1 percent] of 100,000,” Bressers said.

Plus, as other security researchers have documented, the window between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits – often by reverse engineering the patch while end users are still applying the fix – is rapidly shrinking. This is also thanks to AI.

From CVE to KEV

From January to June, 88 percent of the exploitation observed by CrowdStrike using public proof-of-concept (PoC) code occurred within 48 hours of the code's release. The security firm said China-linked groups such as Vault Panda and Genesis Panda moved even faster, launching attacks within 24 hours of disclosure.

Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026. This window has closed even further during the second half of the year, which also seems to coincide with the AI-induced vulnpocalypse.

“It’s often just hours,” Bressers said, noting 14 make-me-root vulnerabilities that VulnCheck disclosed on Friday in Copeland refrigeration controllers. Two are under active exploitation. These are the devices that Iranian hackers abused to spoil food and spark fires in supermarkets across Europe.

“We published those CVEs, and literally minutes later, we were seeing hits on our honey pots,” Bressers said about the Copeland device vulnerabilities. “We’ve hit a point where with anything that looks interesting, someone is taking that information and seeing what they can do with it. Is it AI driven? Probably. It'd be hard to say it's not, because we've seen it really ramp up recently.”

This influx of software bugs requires a sea change in how the entire industry approaches vulnerability disclosure and patching.

“We don't have a security problem anymore,” Bressers said. “We have a data problem now. Instead of obsessing over vulnerabilities, we need to start looking at things like heat maps for infrastructure, and figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you. The CISA BOD helps with that.”

What to prioritize in a patchpocalypse

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) in June issued a cybersecurity directive that replaces flat-deadline vulnerability management policies. Instead of prioritizing patching based solely on CVSS severity scores, the directive instructs organizations to prioritize based on specific risk criteria, including whether the asset is internet-exposed, under active exploitation, and whether an attacker can automate the exploit.

“It's telling people to figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you, and then put those at the top of the list, instead of just saying we're going to fix all the criticals,” Bressers said.

AI-generated vulnerability disclosures also create huge headaches for open source software developers and maintainers, which Bressers describes as a security problem “ super close to my heart.”

“You've got individual developers that are drowning in vulnerability reports,” he said. “You have foundations being crushed by AI agents scraping their data or downloading their packages, millions of times a day, and it's straining the seams absolutely everywhere you look. The one thing I can say with certainty is: The way we currently do things has to change, and it's going to have to change fairly soon.”

Different open source projects have taken different approaches to solving this issue. The Eclipse Foundation, which houses the Open VSX Registry, in April launched a “managed tier” for enterprise customers and other organizations running Open VSX at scale.

Instead of using the free, open source version, the managed version guarantees a 99.95 percent uptime SLA backed by service credits. Its customers include AWS, IBM, Google, Cursor, and Windsurf. This paid option means commercial users who rely on the registry help fund its ongoing maintenance - and their own platforms’ security and performance.

Meanwhile, curl’s maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, citing an “ avalanche of vulnerability reports," updated its bug reporting rules last month. As of October 26, all low- and medium-severity reports go directly into the public GitHub repository, with only the high- and critical-flaws receiving private handling.

Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty program this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team.

“A lot more needs to happen, and I think it is going to be a challenge to enact some of this change,” Bressers said. “When a package registry drastically changes something, people start freaking out, and the world is going to end, and people on LinkedIn are complaining - a lot of people are hesitant. No one wants to be the first to jump into the alligator-filled pool. That's one of our challenges.”®
